Until long past midnight I lingered there, murmurinii prayers and entreaties in vain. More than onee'l tried to break through the funereal hedge; but within the garden it was protected by stout stakes placed aslant each other and firmly flied in the ground. Barrymore was fast asleep when at length, wearied, excited, and half-way between hope and despair, I reached the inn; and, after lying awake for the rest of the night, I resolved to confide in him fully in the morning. Ile was delighted. I could see that he did not quite believe my story, but he resolved to put it into verse form at once. _ _ _

"The idea of your lady-love dying behind the cypress-hedge while you are eating your heart out on the other side and can't get at her is most old-world and touching," he said. "The Queen Anne period will be the best for the verses, J think, and--" "Barrymore, don't be an idiot It was Clare Hayward. What does it all mean ? " "Presumably she is taking a holiday at St. Jacques, as we are doing, and has chosen a nice cpiet house wheue she won't be bothered." "But she has disappeared for nearly for four years. And then the story of the prisoner—and of the lunatic--" "I don't suppose 'Miss Clare Hayward is the sort of girl to be kept anywhere against be, will, from what I saw of her on the one or two occasions when I met her. Besides, we all heard she had eloped—" "Does this look like an elopement? The village people have all told you that only the farmer and his wife and what they call 'a ghost' are to be found at the chateau.'

"Possibly she eloped with the farmer. ,or Heaven's sake talk seriously! You have heard the old couple have lived here -about twenty years, and that they are supposed to be caretakers to this man Devigne, who never names here. We must find out this Devigne, and m tke him release Miss Hayward." "Softly, softly! Would it not be better to ascertain first whether Miss Hayward 'wants to b 3 released ? " _ _ _ _ _

"Do you suppose a lovely, gifted girl of six or s3ven-and-twenty leaves a brilliant stage career t) live alone in a bole, a vault, like that ?" "It dues seem odd. But, my poor Cedric, I see oily one other explanation. She may really be rn.i.d, and her relatives !illy have placed her in nt-traint here."

"It is not possible !". I maintained, stoutly. "No one was ever more sweetly sane than she. Don't you remember her bantering replies to my ardent love-letters—l showed you one or two. l might, indeed, have shewn you them all, much ai I prized them, for she never gave me one word of direct encouragement--" "Still, I think she liked you, Ced. 1 heard shf had a Tartar of a mother. .Perhaps the old lady didn't think you a gcod enough match—" "1 was not. But no one would have been good enough for that peerless girl. She liked me, l really believe, as well as any man; but she owned to me she had never really loved as she felt shE could love. She was a girl of deep, restrained feeling—but mad, never!" "Well, what do you mean to do? " "Haunt the place, paint the place, never leave it until I see her and speak to her. Meantime, we must make inquiries right and left, and hunt this Devine out. • There is eel tainly seine mystery and foul play about this. I believe Clare has been kidnapped, and is detained here against her will--" "By whom? Not a soul ever comes here, SO our landlord says." "I can't argue about it. Nor could you if you felt as I do. lam going now to set up my easel before the cypress-hedge. Don't expect me to dinner. I shall take some food with me. You know the people here—it is your part to ask questions." So I left Barrymore, and for three days early morning found me seated before the cypress- hedge, and moonrise found me wandering round the hidden garden. Once only did I see the wooden door open. A short, heavily-built peasant of apparently some sixty years of age came out, and walked slowly past my easel, staring suspiciousla at me as he did so. I noticed that he lockee the door behind him, that he wore the usual blue linen blouse of French workers, and that he leaned upon a heavy stick. His face appeared sullen and brutal, and when I addressed him he shook his head' and made a sign of being deal as he tramped away. - There was no bell to the door by which he had passed out or any apparent means of communica- tion with the house, and in two hours' time, when the man returned awl casting a glance of surly dis- favour at me unlocked the door and disappeared, I had learnt nothing. That night I tried writing notes to Clare and forcing them through the hedge; but two days more elapsed before any answer came to me. During that time I had learnt from a notary at Greux, to whom Barrymore was referred, that the old, fortified farmhouse, which was supposed to date from the sixteenth century, had belonged to an impoverished French noble, family, from whom it had been purchased some eighteen years ago by a Monsieur Devigne of Paris, who, however, had never lived there, and had not even visited the spot for eight or nine years. As to the imprisoned lady, the notary knew nothing. "Old houses always have silly stories told about them by superstitious peasants," he said. And beyond a promise that he would try to dis- cover Monsieur Devigne's Parisian address, liarrymore could get no more from him. The night afterl received this news my vir of live days and nights was at length rewarded. No note of song 'heralded her coming this time. Suddenly the cypress branches were 'anted, and, as before, her face looked out, with every delicate feature distinct in the moonlight. Quivering with emotion, I crept nearer to the hedge. "Clare! Js it really you ? " I murmured. "By .what right do you use my name ? And why are you here at all ? " "It was accident brought me—or fate. Only tell me you are perfectly happy and contented, that you have no wish to leave this place and be free, and on my honour I a ill not trouble you again
-Sha was silent. Suddenly her face contracted and tears rushed from her eyes.
"Happy! Who is happy;"---she cried, wildly. "Are you .11aPPY "1 can never be happy without you, and you know it."

"Poor boy !" she said, with sudden sweetness, rxing those wonderful dark eyes of hers, misty with tears, upon my face. "I am sorry for you, much seri ier than I ever used to be. But yeu trust go away. Yeti cannot do me any good by staying, and already 'you have done me more harm tint) you can ever repair." "/.' Ido yeu harm! " I repeated in amaze- ment. "Why, I would give my life to serve you. There is nothing you can ask me that I wil! do."
"Then I ycu to Icave this place at once," she said, in quick, carnest tones. "Your being here is the worst thing that can hapren to me. I can never be anything to you, and I must never YOU again."
"Bat you are a prisoner *non-" "Not 7t. hat. "
"Do you wish to leave ?" "Wish!" she rapeated, with sudd(n passion. "Ah, how I wish it! But You cannot help me. Ail you can do for me is to go—and go at once V. "Let me write to you." / “No.
"Let me tell your friends in England,"

, "No, no, no ! By doing anything like that you would destroy my last chance of happiness." "I cannot understand." '"1 cannot explain. Forget that you have ever seen me' and go!" gazed at her pleadingly. It seemed that her face had grown hard and cold.
"If you knew," I murmured, "what love is!" "If I hifir'"
The words broke front her in mournful bitter- ness.. Then the cypress branches closed before her face, and 1 good in the moonlight alone.
Thera Was nothing to do but to obey her and

darrva ore was convinced from what- I told n!m that Clar was dying for love of me; but I knew better, and the mystery was deeper than ever, I would have left St. Jacques the next morning out for a letter I -received from my brilliant Paris Friend, Jean Sanspeur, to whom I had written at his country cottage near Orleans, giving him details of the odd little village of St. Jacques, which I thought might be of use to him in hiA novels.

61-1.3,l start at oleo on my motor and look %no nod vont- roet-friond up." he wrote in English. "A village with a haunted monastery, lovp-garou, and a mysterious château, is worth knowing in these matter-of-fact days. Then :our hint that the 'romance of your life'

div.head: CYPRESS-TIEDGE.
div.p: THE CYPRESS-TIEDGE.
BY GERTRUDE WARDEN,
Author of "Scoundrel or Saint ? " "The Senti- mental Sex," "A Wise and a Foolish Virgin," &c.

"Dear CA—Come to me at once! Here, in the middle of France, between the &Zinc and the Loire, I have discovered the ideal village you and I, as painter and poet, have sought for so long. Needless to say, few people live in it, and it is very difficult to get at. Cominr, from Paris you had better get out at Macon; then you will have a twelve-mile drive in a jolting, ancient diligence from the village of Greux to this delightful spot. No tourist has ever been here. The peasants_ believe I am mad. They

speak an unintelligible patob, and sport among • the vines. The country teems with romance and let,“ena, and you can live like a fighting-cock on a franc a day. Tear yourself, then, from the hollow gaieties of Paris, the bitter jests of Monsieur Jean Sanspeur and the lest of the decadent literary gang, and come to this most lonely and beautiful hamlet, to steep yoursel: in fairy legendary lore—if you are clever enough to understand what the people say! There is a ruined mill, an empty, haunted monastery, a churchyard frequented by a loup-garou, and a ravishing, fortified farmhouse, the turrets of which are just vi,ible .here and there above the most dark, mysterious, awe-inspiring, sketch- and-verse provoking hedge of cypresses, the like of which I have never seen before. And to this last place there is the strangest mystery attached. They say— But I vow you shall not hear what they say until you come! Think of it as subject for your next picture to be rejected by the Royal Academy—a wide, fertile plain a blue line ot low hills in the far di.,4tance, an:..l the eerie even- ing light catching th. 3 turretted roof of the castli hidden behind the funereal hedge, through which a white face peep Title, The Cypress-hedge.' The name of -my village, by the way, is St. Jacques. Come to the little inn kept by -11ronsiem Boulecart, and ask for the -mad Englishman. Thus, and thus only, you will discover your friend,

"BATZT.YMORE BRAY." It was lav when I receive:l this letter. I was eight - and- twenty, staying in . Paris, and immensely attraete,d hy the bitter wit and brilliancy or "Jean Sanspeur," as he called himself, a French _writer- who had recently
scored some remarkable successes by his novel's and plays, each one of ?vhich was written with a view to show his dislike and contempt for women.-

Sanspeur was a celebrity. I was a comparativelN unknown young English painter living on a small private income. I was neither brilliant nor witty. and so far from despising women I had been, and was still, as much in love as it is possible for a man to he. But I was a good listener, and Sanspeur, who was fully twelve years my senior, had taken a fancy to me and endeavoured tc instil into me his ideas.

Now, however, he was leaving Paris, and the idea of joining my old, friend, little, chubby Barrymorc. Bray, in a romantic village attracted inc. After nearly four ycars of it I was as much in love as ever, and I wanted quiet and peace to dream about her. Barrymore was a sympathetic soul, and when I wearied of his constant chatter I left eff listening to it. Then the title and idea, "The Cypress-I-ledge," pleased my humour well. Without. a word of farewell, therefore, I packed my belongings an set off in the early morning from Paris, arriving at the village el' St. Jacques at about half-past five on a still and sultry evening. Barrymore was charmed to receive me. He wazt a short, fat, fresh-coloured, wholesome-lookine man, whom no one would have suspected writing dismal poetry. Supper first, and then the mill and the cypress-hedge was his pro- gramme. .

"You must see. the cypress-hedge first by moonlight," he explained. "And, my boy, if HIE ghostly stillness of the place, the impenetrable thickness of that black barrier, and the mysterious glimpse of the red-roofed turrets it encloses don't fascinate you, then nature is a cheat, and has given you your elegant ,figure, and dreamy blue eyes, and all the rest' of it fox nothing." "But is it inhabited ?"

"An old farmer and his wife have lived there for years. But they are hardly ever seen outside the gates. The peasants never pass the place at night without crossing themselves, and no one is .allowed to enter; but the story goes that the ghost of a murdered lady haunts the grounds, and that at night she may be heard singing in ar unknown tongue." "Have you heard her? " "I? Well, no. You see, I've only 1-een here a week, and with long out-door excursions I get tired and like to go to bed early. But you, m) dear Cedric, are young and enterprising, and agog for adventure. Yam are the knight to inter- view the ghost! Our host here tells me he believes the owner of the house, a man called Devigne, really does keep a lunatic relative shut up in the chateau under the care of the old couple. Who can tell ? But it's remantic—very ! " Romantic indeed I found the place a few hours later, as I stood before the gates of the old chateau in the moonlight. Belted, barred, ane. unused gates of rusty iron they were, and in and 43ut of their interstices brambles clung and twined. No view of the house or garden. \vas obtainable through or over them, for the grass grew long beneath them and cypress branches were intertwined above.

Some way to the left of these gates, however, Barrymore had discovered a sirall, exceeding]) at,:ong wooden door, almost hidden by the hedge, and through this, no doubt, the rainier and-his wire passed on their rare excursions into the village. The cnclosure was a large one, but anything more profoundly -melancholy it was impossible to imagine, and as the night wind faintly stirred the branches of the dark, closely- plaited cypress trees, it seemed as though we were lingering by a huge graveyard. Suddenly Bariymore seized my arm. By the moonlight 1 could see his plump, pink face looked pale and troubled.
- "By Jovel" he whispered. "There a wonlan singing in the gardcn • Sounds uncanny, doun't ?"

Very soft and sad the notes sounded in the moonlight quiet. The voice was a sweet soprano, and the air and words, which I presently caught, were both oddly, even painfully, familiar to me. The last time I had heard them was upon the stage in England, for the song was a pretty bAllad with a " rthain from one of the Gilbert and Sullivan operas, and the singer had been Clare Hayward, a most beautiful cnil fascinating young English actrcs and vocalist, whose portrait I had sketched a lmudred times, and whose image was, and ever would be, clearly printed upon my heart, tholl she had dis- appeared from the London world for nearly four years. _ _
- Not only the song but the voice, tco, I seenaccl to recognise. How could I ever forget Clare Bayward's voice, so -sweet, FO sad, and of so strangely penetrating a quality!

Traabling in every limb -I waited, bangle:: upon each note until the sorg had ceased, to be; followed by a deep, sobbing sigh, so near to where I stood on the other side of the cypress. hedge that it seemed to throb from the singer', heart into mine. "Clare!"

I whispered the name at first in broken accents. Barrymore stared at me, and then, as I believe genuinely frightened, he incontinently Led. "Clare! " I cried again more loudly, and listen- ing in the still' c:s I fancied I could hear the rustle of a woman's dress. Frantic now to discover some means of penetrating that deathlike barrier between us, I hurried backwards and forwards, reeking for some 'Means of effecting an entry into flu mysterious garden. But I strained my eyes with this idea, the dark branches were slowly parted at a spot not far from the wooden door, and through the open- ing thus framed a woman's face peered out at me, white and ghostly in the moonlight. And pale and changed though it was, the once lovely outlines thin and aged, the dark eyes filled- with an unutterable sadness, the face was that of the woman I loved—Clare Hayward!

As suddenly and strangely as she had appeared, re did the woman behind the cypress-hedge vanish. Whether she krow me nnin. whether he even saw me, I could not tell, although her eyes seemed to be fixed for that brief moment opoazziy two.

connected with St. Jacques, .and that you are too much agitated to write coherently, fascinates me. It is to interesting to meet a real flesh-and- blood man- ingenuous enough to love a woman and believe in her, that I must coma and have another look at you before a lucid interval comes to you! I shall have started long before you receive this, and I hope to arrive in your wonderful village Thursday evening." It was Thursday when I received this letter, the day after my interview with Clare. I could not let so distinguished a man as Jean Sanspeur arrive after my departure. so that had to be put off to the next day. The notion of meeting him just now was, nevertheless, supremely dis- tasteful to me. Charming and brilliant as Sanspeur was, his bitterness against women and the cruelty of his constant gibes against them would, I felt, jar upon me terribly at this moment when, between love, pity, and wonder- ment,'l was half-distraught. All that day I wandered about alone, not venturing to approach the château within the cypress-hedge. But as twilight gathered an unwonted excitement in the little village, and the snorting and panting of a motor-ear, apprised me or Sanspeur's coming, and I greeted him at the. door of our inn, before which lie was descending from his motor in the middle of a small crowd stupefied Niith wonder. At the time of which I write Sanspeur was still a youngish-looking Man, of slight build, medium height, and a face which was rathel eager and sensitive in expression than hard and bitter as his writings would have suggested. Of brilliant intellect and the highest cultivation, he could be, when he chose, irresistible to man or woman. As soon as he saw me he began at once on the subject of my "romance." "You have never told me the lady's name or anything about her," he said.. "And how in the world can she be associated with this World- forgotten village in the heart of France?" Being in that humour when an a loves to talk of his griefs, I forthwith detailed to him the whole story of my infatuation for the beautiful Clare Hayward up to the moment when, in hard, despairing tones, she had driven me from her on the preceding evening. "What can I do ha go ? " I asked him. "And yet I am convinced she is .bro i, akin her heart, and I know she is wasting her youth and beauty, and the womanly love and tenderness of which I am sure she is capable, shut up a prisoner within that terrible cypress-hedge, in the care of brutal and ignorant peasants." Sanspeur • turned sharply away, and stared out of the window.
His next words were so irrelevant that they astonished me.

" What is year Christian name, West ? " ho asked, abruptly. "Cedric. Why ? " • "iNothing ! I don't want any supper at present. I shall take leave of you for a few hours and have a turn in the neighbourhood. And, if you don't mind, I shall go alone." Without another word he left the inn, and jumping into his motor by the side of hiE chautThier, . whizzed off down the startled village street. . . _

The remainder of that evening was eventful indeed, and brought me the strangest revelation. In company with Barrymore I went for a last walk in the environs of St. Jacques, and, need- less to say, for a last look at Clare Hayward's urison.

But as I approached the spot where her pale face had first appeared to me peering through the cypress branches, the panting sound of an approaching motor reached my ears. Nearer and,nearer it came, and Barrymore and I were making ready to welcome Sanspeur when a fierce-looking d 0,,, startled by the unexpected sounds, sprang out the hedge and rushed barking to meet the vehicle. • - The accident which -ensued' was the work of a moment. • The driver moved the car pharply on one side to avoid running over the infuriated animal, ami, in less time than it takes to tell it, the carriage and its occupants were flung into a deep, dry ditch on the side of the road. Barrymore and I hurried up in dismay. The ctr was a wreck, the chauffeur was unhurt, but Jean Sanspeur lay insensible, his arm broken beneath him.

it was past eight o'clock. Not a soul was in sight, and we were two miles from the nearest cottage. While Bammore and I were debating how beat to convey our poor friend to St. Jacques, Sanspeur opened his eyes, and with his uninjured arm began fumbling in his pocket, whence he drew forth a key. "The kcof of the door in the cypress hedge, he murmured, faintly. "The house is mine. Mv real name is Devigne, and--" -Forthwith he fainted again, and, dumb with amazement, I took the key he had dropped and unfastened the wooden door, the chauffeur and Barrymore following me with Sanspeur's uncon- scious body. Sweet perfume from may-bushes and garden- lilies.greeted me as the door swung open; but bqore I had time to take note of the mysterious girden a woman's cry rang out, and Clitire herself rushed past me and ilun,* herself on her knees on the narrow path by Lan Sanspeur's 'body. • "Roger! Roger I My husband come back to me at last!" she was sobbing hysterically. "Oh, tell me he is not really hurt, that he will recover! Roger, Roger—my husband!" We left him in her care, and .in that of his old servants, while we went for the nearest doctor. When we returned, Clare, or rather Madame Design°, was seated by her husband's bedside with his hand in hers.

-„... "I have been a mad, jealous fool," Sanspeur owned to me, when the doctor had set his arm and prophesied a speedy 'recovery. "I saw my wife in London nearly four years ago, and within a week persuaded her to marry me. Naturally I would not let her act, and the discovery of a packet of your wild love-letters, .West, sent me into an inane fury. I left her after we had been married • month, vowing that I would not return until I could trust her; and on the allowance my lawyer sent her she, of her own free will, chose to live here, in this farmhouse Iliad bought years ago and told her of, to prove to me that she cared nothing for the world or for society and admiration, and that she would wait for me until I returned to her. In my stupid obstinacy I stayed away. Now, like the angel she is, she has forgiven me. But, though I like you, West, I think she is right, and you had better go home ! " Home, therefore, I went, leaving Clare and her husband absorbed in each other and supremely happy. I hope the experience Made me wiser as well as sadder. I know it brought me luck in a way, for next year I made a success at the 11. A. with a picture which was hung upon the line. And it was called--" The CypresS-Hedge,ni [THE END. I

div.head: CROCODILE TEARS.
div.p: CROCODILE TEARS.
Two Classes Scorned by Sir John Brunner.

At the recent Budget protest meeting at Macclesfield, Colorel Bromley-Davenport made some references to Sir John Brunner. As to his (Sir John's) private character it was said that he was a good-hearted and a kind-hearted man, but on a rolitical platform the Colonel declared him to be one of the most ill- nltured men he Lad ever heard of."
Sir Jan Brunner, replying to the latter reference, asks:
"%\ hat is the fotuAation for this? I sincerely wish to punish, tnd I have Leen perfectly frank about it, two classes of men, __ _ _

"The first is that class which, in the name of Patriotism, howled for more Dreadnoughts, and now howl because they are asked to pay a fair share of taxation. The other is that of the brewers who by tying their houses, despoiled 85,11e0 licensed victuallers of a full half of their livelihood, then sold their breweries to the public at exorbihnt far cy prices and now weep crocodile tears over the widow s,the orptans, and the clergymen among the impoverished sEare- holders.
" I have the most profound contempt for the whole lot of them, and would rather break stones for a living than be one of the latter gang."

div.head: LOOK AT AMERICA.
div.p: LOOK AT AMERICA.

Recent reports of the British Consuls in the United States throw a strong light on the misleading charaz..ter of Tariff Reformers' assertions with regard to the cost of living and the general condition of the workers in that country.
For Instance, our Consul-General at Boston, in his report on the trade of that district in 1008, says :
INCREASED COST OF LIVING

" It is stated by the best authorities that the genera/ cost of living at Boston has increased 42 per cent. during the past seven years." But the Tariff Reformers tell you that if the cost of living has increased, wages have increased more. Here, however, are the facts, as given in the same report :

div.head: NO INCREASE IN WAGES.
div.p: NO INCREASE IN WAGES.
" No permanent rise of earnings proportionate to the above augmentations in prices appears to have taken place."
LIFE A STRUGGLE
Our Consul in Chicago tells us in his report for 1908 :

"To a married man, working on the average salary, life is a struggle at the best of times, and is more so now than formerly, as the cost of living has increased over 30 per cent, in the last ten years."

These-are unbiassed official statements made to our Government by men who know the facts of the condi- tions of life in the United States. They know how little you can trust the pretty pictures which Tariff Reformers paint for you, when they try to per- suade you that Protection has made America a paradise for workers. Here are some details iu regard to prices and the cost of living in Boston, which our Consul supplies.

div.head: To Retail Butchers
div.p: To Retail Butchers
What Does Tariff Reform Mean for Your Business?
WHAT TARIFF REFORMERS PROPOSE.

You know the Tariff Reformers' proposals with regard to meat imports. They want to levy ,a tax on our foreign imports of meat in order to diminish the amount of them. The immediate \result will be to make meat dearer, whether imported or home-grown. When meat for any reason temporarily increases in price, you know that you selfless of it. It is possible to live without eating much meat; and an increase in price, such as taxation will bring about, might induce the poorest of your customers to do without meat altogether ; while these who were better off would inevitably buy less of it

div.head: HIGH PRICES MEAN DIMINISHED SALES.
div.p: HIGH PRICES MEAN DIMINISHED SALES.

What effect has Protection had on meat consumption in Germany? Consular Reports show a considerable reduction in the amount of butchers' meat consumed per head by the population. Between 1901 and 1905, for instance, according to the Report of the U.S.A. Consul at Dresden, there was a decrease of over Mbs. per head in the amount of meat consumed in Germany; and according to our own Consul at Frankfort, the increase in the duties on meat in the new German Tariff of 1900 was followed by a further fall in con- sumption of 51hs. per head in that year. The duty on foreign meat which Tariff Reformers propose would inevitably be followed by a decrease in the amount of meat consumed in this country. You would sell less, and your total profits would be less.

div.head: AND WHAT ABOUT YOUR EXPENSES?
div.p: AND WHAT ABOUT YOUR EXPENSES?

Your own expenses must be increased by Tariff Reform. Just as an import duty would make meat dearer, so the proposed new tariffs would render dearer everything you eat or wear or use. You would have less coming in from your business; and in order to live as you do now, you would inevit- ably have to spend more upon the things you buy. Is that an attractive prospect for you? If not, insist that meat in this country should remain untaxed, and Vote and Work for the continu- ance of

WARRING TON AND DISTRICT ASSOCIATION. BULL'S HEAD WINS THE CROSFIELD CUP.

The final for the handsome cup presented by Mr. A. ll—Crosfield, M.P., in connection with the Warring- ton and District Boss ling Associstion, was held on Saturday last, the match being played on the Cemetery Hotel Green. Bull's Head won the cup for the fourth time, beating Wilson's Hotel, Runcorn, by 75 points, their score being 245 to Wilson's 170. During the afternoon, Sir Gilbert and Lady Greenall,Alderman and Mrs. Smethurst, Mr. and Mrs. Robert Pierpoint, and Alderman John Evans paid a visit to the green and were very keenly interested in the games. The bowling was of a very high order, although in many instances there were good margins. The result was as follows : BULL'S HEAD. WILSON'S HOTEL. T. Hackett J. Swanton 2l T. Woods l2 H. There was another thing, and that was that the bowlini: gr -ns provided a breathing space uhich in a congested area like that could not help but improve the manhood of the t )wn. Lady GREENALL in handing the cap to the winner, said that she must congratulate him upon his excellently fought garae. She was sure they would all agree with her that it. had been well won. (Cheers). div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
Cricket.

Hearty congratulations to the Warrington First Eleven on securing with so much distinction the Championship and Cup for the West Lanca- shire League. Warrington have all through the season shown fine form and it was obvious that they meant amassing the honours for the current term. By going through their League programme undefeated they would seem to be easy winners, but as a matter of fact the ism was in doubt until Saturday, several "moral victories " by Warrington being returned as draws owing to wet weather and the clock. To win outright they had to defeat St.Helens Recreation at St. Helens on Saturday, and this they accomplished with ease. A drawn game would have necessitated them playing off for the Championship with Prescot but this ordeal was avoided.

Silcock, who has captured the team with fine judg- ment throughout the season and done much to main- tain the enthusiasm of the players, took the liberty of putting his opponents in to bat on Saturday. There had been a lot of rain in the morning and the wicket was very soft, but it suited the operations of Creswell and Callon who relieved Warrington of any anxiety by tumbling the Recs out for the small score of 24. It will be remembered that at Warringtoa the Rees had the " honour " of going down for 14 runs, a League record, the Rev. H. Gray getting seven wickets for nine runs. Though he was absent on Saturday, the Recs could not double these figures, Callon getting five wickets for 11, and Cresswell five for 13. The "pro" performed the hat-trick and was loudly cheered.

Warrington made light of the task before them and knocked off the runs for the loss of two wickets, eventually compiling 118 runs for nine, before the rain came on again. It was a fine victory and an excellent wind-up to Warrington's League season.

W. H. Podmore, the veteran of the team, again proved that he is still one of the best by compiing 40 runs in excellent style. Cresswell rattled up a lively 26 and S. Partridge got 16 by promising cricket. J. Callon made 15, so that Warrington's run-getting power was well demonstrated. A. word should be said for the fielding of the champions, which was excellent throughout the Rees' brief stay at the AV icketh.

The second elevens of the two clubs were also engaged in a championship battle, but the result was in favour of the Rees second string who headed the second division after getting Warrington out for 60, and comp:ling 80 runs for half their wickets. War- rington second have struck a lean time, but thEy have young players in their ranks who, should train on in a season or two.

Hard lines on Latchford St. James' (the Warrington and District League Champions) who suffered defelt for the first time for two seasons at the hands of the " Guardian " Office. It is hard to believe that St. St. James' were beaten by such a team that the Printers turn out, but such it wam. But, then the " Guardian " were in fine form and were not over confident, whilst the champions, thinking nobody could equal them were over confident and finished up otherwise. The" Guardian" knocked up a score of 51, two of their players reaching double figures, H. Paton 13, and D. Clarke 10. St. James' only run up the modest number of 31. For the winners, H. Payton bowled splendidly, taking 5 wickets for 7 runs. He performed the hat-trick. D Clarke got 2 wTokets for 5 runs, and L. Riley 3 for 12. J. Hallam was the most effective with the ball for St. James' and captured 5 wickets for 24 runs.

Walker's Brewery vanquished the Cheshire Lines Engineers, the former scoring 79 and the latter 58. J. Molloy for the Brewery knocked up the splendid score of 28 and C Turner and W. Rylance scored 12 and 10 respectfully. Duckworth played well for the Engineers, scoring 21. McKay was the other man who reached double figures, his total being 13. Rylance bowled well for the Brewers, capturing six wickets, whilst McKay for the Engineers was respon- sible for five wickets.

Latchford Bantists had an easy time of it, triumph- ing over Whitecross by 31 runs, the scoring being 49 and 18 respectfully. During the whole match only one man (A. Starkey, Baptists) got to the double number, his scoring being a modest 13, H. Wright accomplished a brilliant bowling performance, taking 10 wickets for 21 runs. A. Fletcher, for Latchford, captured six wickets for 10 runs and J. Conway three for six.

Wilderspool Brewery suffered defeat at the hands of Sankey Wire Mills.. The former knocked up 23, which was followed by the latter's 40. The best batting was done by Bell (Wire Mills) who scored 23. He also was very effective with the ball, taking six wickets for five runs, whilst Hawthorne (NTre 'Mills) took four for 18.. ' •

Padgate played Sankey. The former raised 12 between them, whilst the latter just managed to double that number. Webb and Forster, for Sankey, bowled well, taking five wickets for four and five for eight respectively.

Winwick. Asylum had an easy task with Haydock Lodge beating them by 66 runs. The former's score was 131 for seven wickets and the lalter's 65 all out. Dr. Ferguson (Asylum) was the mast brilliant bats- man, scoring 63 not out. G.Floyd (Asylum) also played well, his total being 21. For Haydock Lodge J. Noble was the most successful, knocking up a hand- some 31. W. Sanderson (Asylum) secured seven wickets for 20 runs.

div.head: Bowling.
div.p: Bowling.

Some very good games were witnessed at Peel Green on Saturday last, when Warrington Workshops were defeated by Eccles Workshops by 108. Of course, Warrington's team was not particularly strong owing to the individual merit .competition taking place. The best wins were obtained by 11. Mears and S. Bethel (Eccles) who each won 15-2. G. Bethel, another brother, had also a big win, his opponent (R. Clarke, Greening's) only registering 5 points. Each side consisted of 39 players. The Eccles team scored 479 against 371 by their opponents, and had 25 winners against Warrington's 11.

Last Saturday the individual merit competition in connection with the Warrington .Works Bowling Association was resumed and some very good games ensued. Joe Gleave for P. and K gained a splendid victory over W. Rostron defeating him by 9. The greatest disparity in the scores was H Wilson 15 to A. Harrison 5.
The competition will be continued to-day (Saturday) when some very keen competition is expected. Such players as A. Scott, Jack Gleave and Ted Gleave (all scratch) ought to draw many spectators.
Bravo Bull's Head ! Bull's Head have again won the handsome trophy presented by Mr. A. H. Crosfield, MT., beating Wilson's Hotel on Saturday last on the

'Cemetery Hotel green by 75 points, the score being 245 and 170.A1l the Warrington men except W.Simister had the good fortune to reach the reluired number 21. However, Simister may be pardoned on the ground th it he was only one point behind.Perhaps'one of the easiest games of the afternoon was between A. Gleave(Bull's Head) and G.Woods. The former lead all the way and had an advantage of 11 when his opponent had to be content with 2. Gleave kept pegging away and as a result won by the handsome margin of 12.

There was a good muster present at_the King and Queen to witness the competition in connection with the Constitution Lodge of the Manchester Unity of Oddfellows for the cup presented by P.P.G.M. Thomas Steel. Some very keen games were played, Mr. Steel himself having a good try for it, but he was defeated in the third round by one point by G. Holland, last year's winner. T. Howard won the cup by a majority of five, after a hardly-fought battle with H. Savory,

div.head: Rugby Football.
div.p: Rugby Football.

There are not many sensations stirring in •local football circles. The players are putting in plenty of practice, and there was a particularly good turn-out on Tuesday evening. Another practice will be held at 6 o'clock this afternoon.

Frawley and Brooks are getting nicely over their injuries and should both be fit for the opening match. So far nothing has been heard of O'Malley, but no credence is put in the rumour that he was on board the • ill-fated Waratali. This week-end mail may bring news of him, but he was not expected any earlier.

O'Neill is not likely to be seen here for the opening of the season, if at all, and Dowell also has got out of touch with. the Club. Shugars and J. Jenkins are expected to be back in good time, and no effort is being spared to strengthen the side in other directions.
The member's cards will be on sale on Thursday and Friday evening next and may be obtained from the hon. treasurer, Mr. T. Pemberton,Bewsey Chambers, Bewsey-street, between the hours of 7 and 0.
The Committee have again selected G-. DickenFon as Captain of the Ist team, with E. Brooks for his deputy, whilst J. Lloyd has been elected Captain of the "A" team.

The official times for Northern-Union matches for the season have been.al•ered as follow : September Ist to October 15th, 3.30 p.m. October 16th to November 15th, 3.0 p.m: Novepaber 16th to January 15th, 2.45 p.m. , January 16th to February 15th, 3.0 p.m. February 16th to end of season, 3 30 p.m.

div.head: WATER POLO.
div.p: WATER POLO.
WARRINGTON v. BIRKENHEAD.

These teams met in a Liverpool and District League match at the Corporation Baths, Legh-street, Warring- ton, last night, before a moderate attendance. The visitors had the advantage of the shallow end in the first half. From the throw-in, (*oaten, the Birkenhead fast swimmer, gained possession, and from subsequent play the W: r:ington custodian was severely tested, but managed to keep his goal intact. Warrington assumed the aggressive and after Tumor had failed to beat Rhodes, a long shot from Pepper opened Warrington's account. •This success roused the vhiting team, who raided the home half, and Goalen was again prominent, and easily beat Woods from short range. After this Warrington had rarely a lcok-in. Leyland added No. 2 in quick style. Goals followed in quick succession, Marsden, Goalen, and Leyland making the total five before the interval. On rcsuming, Warrington played much better Turner increasing the score after smart work, and the deficit was further decreased by Pepper, who added the locals' third goal. Even play followed, Birkenhead making strenuous efforts to increase their score. Eventually Goalen scored, making his third. Not to be denied, Warrington raided the visitors end, and Turner again scored. Play now waxed fast and furious and Pepper and Turner again scored for Warrington, whilst Goalen and Leyland made the Birkenhead total eight. Result: Birkenhead 8, Wet rington 6. In addition to the game the two Squadron races were swum between the Co-operative Stores and Crosfield's and the Corporation and Rylands. As Rylands' did not appear the Corporation claimed the game, Crostields also woo their race. A squadron race between Warrington and Birkenhead ended in a victory for the latter.

div.head: DAYLIGHT SAVING BILL'S FATE.
div.p: DAYLIGHT SAVING BILL'S FATE.
Brief Conclusions

It is understood that the report of the Select Corn- mittee who have decided against the Daylight Saving Bill will be one of the shortest—apart from the records of evidence and the appendices—which has ever been presented to the House of Commons have regard to the duration of the inquiry. It occupies only about twenty lines, and the decision with reasons are expressed in sixty words. The thres main paragraphs are as follows: Having regard to the great diversity of opinion existing upon the proposals of the bill and to the grave doubts which have been expressed as to whether the objects of the measure can be attained by legislation without giving rise in cases involving important interests to serious inconvenience. Your committee recommend that the bill be not furtherproceeded with. Your committee, however, desire to record the appreciation of the efforts of those connected with the movement, and particularly those of Mr. Willett, since owing to those efforts the hours of beginning and leaving off work have already been advanced in many cases. Your commit tee further desire to express their indebtedness to Sir H. B ibington Smith and Mr. G. ft. Askwith and the other witnesses for the valuable assistance and information which they have rendered in the course of the inquiry. The remaining few lines of the report are taken up with an intimation that the committee have directed the minutes of evidence and the appendices to be laid before that house. BILL TO BE RE-FRAMED.
Interviewed on Wednesday Mr. Willett, the pro- moter of the Daylight Saving scheme, said the bill is to be framed anew for next session.

Last week Sir Gilbert ANOTHER DEATH- Greenall said that the KNELL land proposals of the Budget sounded the death-knell of pedigree stock-breeding in this country. We hope no one believed him. But we are glad to find that he is not the sole proprietor of death-knells. Colonel Seely possesses one, and this also is. related to the Budget. Speaking at Accrington on Thursday evening, Colonel Seely said: "This Budget is the death-knell of Tariff Reform." Colonel Seely's death-knell has the advantage of being supported by unmis- takable evidence in all directions. Sir Gilbert's sounded a bit cracked!

The strictures recently SCHOOL HYGIENE. passed by the Medical Officer on the un-hygienic state of the elementary schools in the Borough have already borne good fruit. The defects of the various schools have been reported upon, and the Medical Inspection Committee has specified the alterations required in each school, and requested that the school managers be pressed to carry out the suggested improvements. Nearly every one of the old schools is defective in some part of its arrangements, and if all the suggestions are carried out the managers will have quite a busy time. Lighting and ventilation are points which have received most attention; new windows are necessary, and many existing windows have to be made to open; while there are several very necessary recom- mendations in regard to sanitary conveniences. We hope the School Managers will meet the the Committee in the right spirit and not disregard the suggestions as mere fads. Any- one who visits the schools when in use can- not fail to be struck with the stuffy conditions under which thousands of scholars are endeavouring to work. In all probability the results would be better if the youngsters had less cramming and more air and bright- ness during school hours.
During this week the THE COMING House of Commons has HIGH LICENCES. had a rest from the

Budget, and both sides have taken a holiday, but the fighting will begin again in a few days, and this time it will pass on to the Licensing Duties.' It is notorious that the town public-houses in England pay an extraordinarily low licence duty, especially the large public-houses. The new licence duties proposed by the Govern- ment in the Budget Bill will equalise the licences between the big public-houses and the small. At present there is a scandalous inequality. The small public-houses pay very heavily, and the big public-houses pay very lightly. Let us compare London and New York in the matter of licences. The London public- house pays on an average in licence duties only £3B. The public-house of Greater New York pays £205. London, as a whole, pays only £200,000 in revenue on her licences, while New York pays £2,200,000. Last year the Government offered to leave the brewers alone if they would limit their licences for the good of the community on the lines of the report of the Licensing Commission. They refused, and under the leadership of Lord Rothschild they induced the House of Lords to throw out the Licensing Bill. They preferred to keep the 30,000 licences above the proper limit, which, according to the Licensing Commission, exist in England. Having, therefore, preferred to keep those licences they must pay duty on them. They cannot have it every way. •

Amongst the fifteen EPOCH-MAKING measures which Mr. LEGISLATION. Asquith indicated, in making the statement of the Government's intentions at this time of year, as either having obtained the Royal Assent or being practically ready for the Royal Assent, the India Councils, the South Africa Bill, the Labour Exchanges Bill, and the Trade Boards Bill are all measures of first-class importance. Both the South Africa Bill and the India Councils Bill can claim, without the slightest vestige of exaggeration, the title of epoch-making turning-points in Imperial development. The Labour Exchanges Bill and Trade Boards Bill, together with Mr. Burns's' Housing and Town Planning Bill,and the Chancellor of the Exchequer's Development Bill, embody a notable contribution to that policy of social organization which the Government has conceived, and which the Opposition, after first denouncing as Socialistic, now mani- festly envies and would like to appropriate. It is a policy which, steadily and cohsistently reared on the foundations laid in the Old Age Pensions Act and the Budget, will transform the face of our country and open up an almost illimitable vista of national growth and improvement.

Almost any one of AN UNCONSCIOUS these measures would TRIBUTE. have been thought sufficient to justify 'marking time" in the rest of a session when Mr. Balfour used to inform his followers that they would not be burdened with over- much legislation. Mr. Lyttleton paid a tribute—all the more flattering because unconscious—to the Government's extra- ordinary record of constructive work when he endeavoured to claim credit for the Opposition as having co-operated with the Government by giving to their measures the handsomest treatment." Indeed, as Mr. Asquith chaffingly remarked,the Opposi- tion are evidently preparing to claim a partnership in the Budget which they have denounced and obstructed. Mr. Lyttleton declared that the Budget had been almost remodelled" though their efforts. It is high time that the Budget Protest League— which is afraid to submit resolutions of protest at its meetings—should drop out of existence, for why should they protest against a Budget which has been "almost remodelled" by the Conservatives them- selves?

Efforts are being made "NOT CRICKET." in certain quarters to persuade Bardsley, the most brilliant bat in this year's Australian team, to remain in England as a county cricketer. Should he care to do so he could no doubt make his •choice between pro- fessionalism and paid amateurism. Some of the counties would be quite willing to create for him one of those comfortable deputy-sub- assistant-secretaryships o£ which we have heard so much in recent years. But we sincerely trust that Mr. Bardsley will not follow the example of several other Colonial cricketers who have come over here with visiting teams and stayed—for a considera- tion. From every point of view this sort of thing is undesirable. In the frrst place it may, if generally approved, ultimately lead to the extension of the principle, to this country of the omnipo- tence of cash in the cricket world,the tempta- tion of men from poor clubs by rich clubs, until, as in the realm of professional foot- ball, the long purse is the essential of pre- eminence. Again,a great deal of the interest of the county championship hitherto has attached to the fact that most county teams

are composed of men who have real, not artificial qualifications to play for the respective counties. And,lastly,if the Colonies find that,sending teams here simply ends in losing their best men to us, they will, if they have the spirit we believe they have, refuse point-blank to send us any more. Of course, if an Australian or a South African would be changing his home anyhow, we should be only too delighted to welcome him in our midst. Should Mr. Bardsley or any of his comrades be coming to live in England for private reasons, we should be extremely pleased to adopt him, and rejoice at the enrichment of English cricket. But that would be merely a happy accident; what we object to is this vulgar, commercial, unsports- manlike scheming to acquire other people's men by holding out tempting baits to them, and this greedy, covetous eye which cannot see a good thing in anyone else's possession without wishing to get hold of it. These things, to use the hallowed phrase, are "not cricket."
On the face of it, what THE STATE AND could be more fantastic THE INSECT. than that the Govern-

ment of the greatest Empire the world has ever seen should con- cern itself with insects? Yet his Majesty's advisers have set up a scientific committee to urge the multiplication of show cases of entomological specimens. The part played by insects in the spread of disease has been recognised in the last decade as never before, and we know now that in the case of diseases, both in men and animals, in Tropical Africa insects arethe agents with which we must deal in order to stamp out the scourge. It is proved, for instance, that men may live immune in malarial districts, so long as they occupy after nightfall mosquito- proof houses. Mosquitoes, on the other hand, sent from these localities have bred malaria in a West-End bedroom. There is the intimate relation, too, between certain insects and economic plants. These matters need to be searched into. In bulk the insect may be contemptible, but his works are great. He brought the construction of the Panama Canal to a standstill, and it was only when the American Government had spent enough to fit out an expedition, and had waged exterminating war on the beast, that yellow fever was stamped out and the works could begin again. If settlement in Africa is to be continued, we must come to grips with the flying and creeping things which, in some cases, can hold the country against us. Lord Cromer will act as Presi- dent af the African Entomological Research Committee, and a better President could hardly be found, for Lord Cromer knows the sulbect in all its bearings, and has seen the splendid work which has been d6ne at the University of Khartoum. Trained entomo- logists will be despatched to the east and west sides of Tropical Africa, and the tracking of noxious insects and the dissemination of instruction in scientific methods of dealing with the pets will become the main business of life of a considerable body of experts. Collections and observations will be made and communicated to the Committee, and these collections will be classified by a number of British and, in some instances, Continental entomologists. Named specimens will be distributed eventually to such institutions as need them for the purpose, of instruction. The work is an important one, and will need to be carefully done. It will afford, we must hope, yet another instance of science's perpetual lesson of the magnificent work that may be done through the taking of infinite pains.

div.head: EXAMNIER,
div.p: THE EXAMNIER,
S ITURDAY AUGUST 28th. 1909.
The performances at THE the Rheims Aeroplane FLYING MEN. Race Meeting have, to

use the classic phrase, "staggered humanity." In the presence of thousands of people the " aviators " have fluttered about in the air six and seven at a time. They have remained up for whole hours, and they have covered the ten kilo- metre course at rates of thirty and forty miles an hour. They have mounted hun- dreds of feet in the air; and skimmedz_along near the ground with the grace and facility of swallows. All manner of startling, evolu- tions have been performed by them; quick turns, rapid ascents, rapid (albeit sometimes too rapid) descents. At one moment a "fly- ing man" has charged full tilt towards the crowd, spreading consternation ;•only to show, by rising and soaring over the people's heads, how complete was his control of his machine. At another he has flown close to a companion, nose and nose, or .crossed:•just above him—a feat the posibility of which was in doubt until now. Needless to say,the machines have been revealed as far from perfect. But,their performances have been great enough to give the world one of the biggest" thrills" it has ever had in time o peace.

How astonishing, as also how instructive has been the progress of this science of flying on heavier-than-air machines! It cannot be more than six years since the first aeroplanist rose from the earth, and the whole story of the rapid development of this last of the world's wonders reads like a chapter out of Mr. H. 0-. WELLS. First we had SANTOS- DumoNT—even that seems but a thing of yesterday—making his gallant little flights in Paris. Then came rumours, vague and unbelieved rumours, of flights made by two taciturn and secretive brothers named WRIGHT in a secluded Ohio countryside. FARMAN was the next to achieve fame. The startling photographs of his machine in the air which were scattered broadcast prepared us for the events which have been crowded into the last twelve months—the visit of the WRIGHTS to Europe, their high-speed flights and dexter- ous gambols at great altitudes in their two- deckers, the rival efforts Of DELAGRANGE and LATHAM, the great time-record of Som- mer, who stayed two hours and more in the air, the gallant failure of LATHAM to cross the Channel, the triumphant success of BLERIOT in compassing that feat. To those with eyes to see the last few months have witnessed achievements which deserve to the full that much-abused term "epoch- making." The Rheims meeting set a seal on them, and woke the continents up. All kinds of machines—monoplanes, biplanes, triplanes —though yet in their infancy, are seen to be easily navigable. Improvements are inevit- able, as inevitable as they always are when man having mastered a great mechanical principle turns his attention to details. The human race, in fact, has attained the desire it has cherished since the dawn of time; henceforth it will know what it is to emulate the birds.

We of pedestrian minds and habits have to face the situation. Owing to the ability and curiosity of men of more enterprise than ourselves it will be our fate henceforth to live in a very changed world. We do not think we are making a wild assumption in saying that within a year the pleasure aeroplane will have appeared in• England, and that within two years this form of carriage will be tolerably plentiful. The question is Will it ever be intolerably plentiful? We confess that we share to some extent the trepidant feelings of those who fear that man's enterprise will be the Undoing of him. We do not anticipate with much pleasure the prospect of mammoth black cock-chafers straddling across the quiet sun- sets with which we are wont to commune at times ; and, if the sky fills up, people who are " in city. pent" will feel more closed in and suffocated than ever. But there is always the chance that one's apprehension may prove baseless. After all, only a very small proportion of our commercial traffic could be carried on in the ethereal blue, and the sec- tion of the community which gees long journeys very often is not large. The pleasure-trippers, too, if they retain their present gregarious tendencies, will flock together in a few favoured spots. So there is quite a chance that most of our beauty- spots will only occasionally be haunted by propellers and canvas wings.

Mr. W. E. Harvey, M.P., for North-East Derbyshire, is Announced to speak at the open-air meeting on Monday evening. The bluff, straightforward Miners' representative should be a great attraction. It is not generally known, but we are able to say with authority that Mr. Ilb,rvey exercised con- siderable influence in averting quite recently the threatened strike in the coal trade. We hope the friends of Progress will give him a hearty cheer on Monday. * * *

A curious point arose in a licensing prose- cution at Runcorn on Monday, when the landlord of the Castle Hotel, Halton, was summoned for serving four men on Sunday, August Bth, who had not passed the three- mile limit. The men came from Widnes,and the evidence showed that the police had measured the shortest route—across the Transporter Bridge. Mr. A. Browne success- fully contended that this was not a highway, and the case was dismissed. * * *

A young married gentleman in the North, returning home one evening, found most of the-rooms on the ground floor- flooded, and the new carpets in a general state of soak, A water-pipe had burst. "My dear 1 " he exclaimed to his wife, "why on earth didn't you just hammer the pipe up? All these things will be ruined. Why ever—here, give me* the hammer! It's so perfectly simple. Now, wait here a minute." He plunged into the cellar, and in a twinkling pounded that pipe flat. Then he heard a sweet voice calling to him from the head of the cellar steps, and saying, "Howard, the gas has gone out,and the water is still running, dear." The moral of this story is, "Learn to hasten slowly, or send for a plumber."

Most of the Tory open-air meetings in Warrington have been failures when judged by the standard of the Monday night gather- ings of Progressives., Several have been abandoned and others most sparsely attended, whereas both Free Trade and the Budget have boomed on the other platform. On Thursday evening the Tories pursued their wearisome course and , Alderman Bennett gallantly presided over a small gathering of people, most of whom insisted on ignoring Tariff Reform and putting questions about the Budget. The Tariff Reformers were so disconcerted that they failed to put their own resolution to the meeting. In order that it should not be entirely unproductive, someone in the audience called for—" Three cheers for the Budget "—which were very heartily given. * *

We can well recall the unholy joy of catapulting a stone right through the glass of a gas-lamp in the days of our youth. Not being found out, we were not punished— which is a pity. The evil practice has grown since those days, and the amount of punish- ment does not seem to fit the crime. A. youth was haled before the local magis- trates on Monday and fined for lamp-break- ing, and in the course of the hearing an official of the Gas Department said it cost them £l5O per year for breakages. The wilful breaking of lamps was worst in the Bewsey district, and the particular lamp mentioned in the case had been broken five times during the last six weeks. During a year the total number of lamps broken was 2,044, and the number of incandescent mantles, 2,818. More vigilance on the part of both parents and police is obviously necessary.

One:sixth only of the population of Prussia had in 1908 a sufficient income (£45 per annum) to place them in the category of income tax payers. When we remember that in arriving at the figure of £45 for each earner, the value of board, lodging, food, and even tips of the worker have to be included, we fail to see any very remarkable evidence in these figures of the great and widespread prosperity which we are assured by the Tariff Reformers is so noticeable all over Germany. * * *

Dr. Dawson Burns, whose death was announced on Monday was a veteran among teetotalers. It was in the General Baptist Chapel, Edgware-road, of which his father was for many years minister, that as a lad of ten years he took the pledge in February 1839. Only few men can proclaim an unbroken record as abstainers for so long a period. Dr. Burns did an immense amount of work as a Temperance advocate. His department as an expert was that of Tem- perance statistics, his annual report being regarded as an authoritative document on the subject. * * *

A return of na,val expenditure which issued this week brings out some of the principal facts of the increasing drain upon the differ- ent Powers. Since 1900-1 our own expendi- ture has grown from thirty millions to £35,142,000. In the same time Germany has increased from £7,648,000 to .E 19,538,00 a pace that has no parallel in Europe. Great Britain, the United States and Ger- many are all spending over ten millions sterling on new construction during the current financial year. France alone among the greater Powers has been Content to rest from the competition. Her total expenditure in 1900 was £14,955,000. Nine years later it is £13,353,000. The United States has more than doubled its expenditure in ten 'years, and contemplates adding to its annual Budget. * * *

While the Budget -debate pauses in the House of Commons, in .the country it goes on as strongly as ever, and it still turns very largely on the land taxes. Those taxes are clearly popular. Meetings are pronouncing in their favour all over the country, and it is difficult indeed for those who oppose them to carry their resolutions. We strongly deprecate any disorder at these Budget Protest meetings, as we are of opinion that the objections to the Budget only require to be stated in order to be refuted. It is quite certain that nothing has done the Budget so much good as the extraordinary display of selfishness on the part of the very wealthy landowners who have been asked to pay their share of taxation. * * *

But these gentlemen do not seem to have learnt wisdom from the attitude of the country. Here is Lord Londonderry, who certainly ought to know better. He is an extremely wealthy man. He owns over 50,000 acres ; one big house in London; two in the English provinces; and one in Ireland. He draws immense revenues in mining royalties, and a large income as a coal merchant and a wharf-owner. There are few richer men in England. And yet this very rich man, instead of bravely under- taking to pay his share, like Lord Lathom, practically threatens to imitate the Dukes by cutting down the expenditure on his estate. He goes down to one of his proper- ties and practically threatens to reduce employment. * * *

On reading this speech it is impossible to avoid one reflection. Here is a nobleman, not a bad nobleman, but a public-spirited man up to his lights, who, when faced with new taxation, seems to have no idea how to recoup except by dismissing employes. But is there no other way out of his difficulties? Take the case of Lord Carrington. When he came into his estates he found himself with three country houses, and decided that he wanted only one to live in. He promptly sold two, and both those houses are now occupied instead of being empty. Lord Londonderry owns five, houses, and at any given time four of them must be empty. Is there not a way out here? * *

Where Lord Londonderry talks more in sorrow than in anger Lord Wemyss does not talk at all, but acts, and acts in anger. Lord Wemyss has, it aapears, closed all his property to the public in the neighbourhood of the town of Peebles. He thinks that he can bring a great town to its knees by a policy of bullying. We think that he is wrong. These great noblemen are mistak- ing the spirit of modern England. What Lord Wemyss will do will not be to bring Peebles to its knees, but to turn the people of Peebles into Socialists. If that is his object, then he is going the right way about to carry it out. The only chance of prevent- ing it is for the Liberals to show that they can prevent a great landlord from defying the public and abusing his rights.

The Marquess of Tullibardine,who happens to be a Unionist candidate in a Scotch town, is wiser than Lord Wemyss. He has found out in his electioneering experiences that a nobleman must justify himself in the possession of his property; so he has invited a party of working men to go over his deer forest at Atholl and issue a report as to whether he is putting it to its best possible use. But we really do not know what he is driving at. Deer forests unhappily are not taxed under the Budget Bill; certainly not deer forests like the Forest of Athol The real question in regard to deer forests is quite another thing. it is whether these great spaces of vacant forest land would not be better used by being afforested than by being devoted simply to the sport of killing deer. * * *

The circulation by the Budget League of over four million leaflets in explanation of the Government's financial proposals is, perhaps the greatest effoit yet put forward in this country in the way of spreading broadcast political "literature." It has been accustomed to be thought that the Anti-Corn Law League were the earliest to adopt .this method of persuading the people; but it is to be traced to the period of "the Fifteen," when "the rebel lords" were making much trouble in Scotland against the House of Hanover, and the North of England—and notably Preston—showed alarming symptoms of revolt. The Whigs were the first in the field in the politico-literary direction; and in Steele's organ, the "Flying Post," a loyal pamphlet was advertized with the note To encourage the free Distribution of this Book in the Country, and that every House- Keeper with a small Charge may be possess'd of this valuable Work, this Pamphlet is sold for Sixpence, tho' the Charge of it amounts to the Price of a Twelvepenny one." Two months later another and even more loyal deliverance was announced for widespread distribution in the same journal in the words, "And that this may be dispers'd to all the Protestaht Associators of Great Britain, those Gentlemen that buy them to give away shall have 300 for 51. and if they take 900, the Author will give tO the Purchaser 100 of them gratis, at his own Charge, provided those that purchase the 900, buy them purely to give away (and not to sell) to the AsSocia- tors." And from this beginning' much has since come.

The annual Plant and Flower Show held in con- nection with the Beautiful Warrington Society will take place to-day in the Drill Hall, and will be opened by Mr. William Long at 2.30 p.m. The Stockton Heath Garden Society's Orchestra will be in attend- ance. Warrington Citizens' Temperance League. A Council meeting of the Warrington Citizens' Temperance League was held on Thursday evening in the Winmarleigi Cafe, Mr. Janies Dodds presiding over a good attendance.—lt was unanimously decided. to convene a Conference for October 7th, to be addressed by Mr. Robert Cameron, M.P., Mr. John Upson and Rev. C. Harvey Cook, on various aspects of temperance work. Further particulars of the Con- ference,over which Mrs. James Dodds, president of the Warrington Band of Hope, will be asked to preside, will be issued later. div.head: . – ton.—Advt. Wedding at St. Paul's Church.
div.p: . - ton.—Advt. Wedding at St. Paul's Church.

A pretty wedding took place at St. Paul's Church, on Thursday when•the contracting parties were Mr. Thomas Emmett, son of Mr. Alfred Emmett, 18, Paul- street, and Miss Edith Manche Warburton, daughter of Mr. Peter Warburton, 92, Bewsey-road. The Rev. W. Bracecamp officiated. The- bride, who was given away by her brother, Mr. James A. Warburton, was dressed in a grey and white costume with hat to match, and carried an ivory prayer book. Miss Beatriee- Warburton, sister of the bride, acted as bridesmaid, and was attired in a pale grey costume. Mr. John Emniett, brother of the bridegroom, dis- charged the duties of best man. After the service the reception was held at the bride's home and later the happy couple left for Llandudno where the honeymoon is being spent. The bride wore a rose-ccloured travelling dress and cream coat with hat to match. The New School iO7 St. Austin's Ward. At a meeting of the Sites and Building Committee of the Education Committee a communication was submitted from the Board of Education, intimating that all the requirements of section 8 of the Educa- tion Act, 1902, having now been duly fulfilled, the Board are prepared to consider the Committee's pro- posal, for the provision'of a new public elementary school in Evelyn-street to be conducted as a Council school for about 1,260 children. The Director submitted to the Committee at a special meeting held yesterday draft conditions for an architectural competition for the erection of this school and the conditions were approved.—Owing to the over-crowd- ing of the senior departments in the schools since the holidays the School Management Committee has urged the Sites and Buildings Committee to proceed as quickly as possible with the provision of the addi- tional school accomm oda ti un required. Beautiful Warrington Society. _ - - - _

The fourth annual show of the -Society will be held this afternoon in the Drill Hall. We are informed that a good number of entries have been received and there is likely to be keen competition in the various claSses. In addition there will be several interesting exhibits, consisting of groups of plants kindly lent by the .Warrington Corporation and various ladies and gentlemen interested in the Society including an exhibi- tion of flowers grown by the scholars of the Beamont School in the school gardens. The children's plants which have won prizes at the various schools will also attract attention and the young prize winners will again compete against each other for medals which have been kindly presented by Lady Greenall. The show will be opened by Mr. William Long, J.P., at 2.30 p.m. and a representative gathering is expected_ During the afternoon and evening the Stockton Heath Garden Society's Orchestt a will play selections and songs will be rendered by Miss E. Taylor, Miss J. Armstrong and Mr. F. Fieldhouse. Tea and refresh- ments will be provided by Mrs. Powis. The show will be well worth a visit and a good attendance of the public is anticipated. _ TRAVELLING TRUNKS, DRESS BASKETS, SUIT
CASES, etc. Prices to sift all.—J. S. GARLAIM, 51, Bridge et., Warrington.—Advt. Concert by the Band of H.M. Irish Guards.

On Mon4a-y the band of H.M. Irish Guards gave two concerts in Parr Hall in the afternoon and even- ing, by permission of tol. G. C. Nugent, M.V.0., and under the conductorship of Mr. Charles Hassell. There was only a small audience in the afternoon, but in the evening the attendance was better, especially in the large back gallery, which is certainly an advantageous place in which to listen to music of brass and military bands. The playing of the pieces com- prised in the afternoon programme (which was the one we were privileged to listen to) was of a high order, the finished Execution and artistic taste discerned in each and all of them clearly indicating that in this band there is an assemblage of master musicians, Three of the p:eces—the two overtures "Merry Wives of Windsor" and " Taannhauser " and the prelude to Act 3 of " Lohengrin "—may be regarded as fair trials of the all-round capability of a combination of brass and ' wood-wind instruments known as the military band, and the proper test of excellence would of course be, how far and how truthfully they could interpret the orchestral score of these pieces. Judged by such a standard it is marvellous that so great an amount of musical " colour " can be thus obtained, and the realisation of these possibilities by the audience was clearly marked by enthusiastic applause. Sergeant Hunt played the melody of Tosti's song "My dreams to the accompaniment of his fellow musicians in grand style, while an item which gave agreeable variety to, the programme was the selection of "Musical Snap- shots "from the pen of the conductor. 1. 1 •-• At the Borough Police Court, on Tuesday. Henry F.:.ulkner, a labourer, was charged with neglecting his six children in a manner likely to cause them unneces- sary suffering end injury to health.—Mr. A. Browne, who appeared for Mrs. Faulkner, said that the man -would not work. He had bad good situations, but had lost them all through drink. He bad a family of nine children, all described by Inspector Cox as healthy children, but who were entirely short of food. The chief witnesses in the case would be prisoner's wife and eldest son aged 21. During the la.st three months be bad not given his wife more than is. per week. Prisoner bad been warned by Inspector Cox, of the N.S.P.C.C., and Mr. Firth (the Police Court Misssonary) had done everything re.ssible to bring about a reconciliation. The children would have been starved, but for two of the sons, who brought in 255, a week,out of which eleven had to be kept. Mrs. Faulkner was in danger of her life, as prisoner bad threatened to alltiot her if she took proceedings against him. She believed that he would. flings had come to such a climax that the neighbours and daughters had complained, and they wanted a stop putting to it. There was no doubt that the children were in actual suffering from hunger and neglected in such a way as to endanger their health by the prisoner going home and frightening them out of their wits. Prismer had been a constable in the Court and also a bailiff at the County Court.--Nfrs. Faulkner corrobo- rated and said that her husband had not given her more than Is. during the last six months. He challengiid her sun to fight on the 17th August. Ihey had nothing else to eat but bread.—Prisoner, who was arrested on a warrant, said he was very sorry that be was in such a position. He had been out of work and was unable to get money to give to his wife. His wife had only spoken of the last few weeks, but he admitted that be had done wrong. He bad work to go to that morning. Ile blamed drink and said he would not touch it again. After hearing prisoner's character, that of having been twelve times previously before the Court for drunkenness, assault and pachiug, the Bench sen- tenced him to one month's imprisonment. THE CHARGE AGAINST A FOOTBALLER. A FURTHER REMAND.

John Cheaters of Charles-street, was again brought up at the Borough Police Court on Tuesday on the serious charge of doing grievously Lodily harm to John Rowan of Hale-street, by fracturing his jaw with his fist. Caief Inspector Williamson in asking for a further remind of seven days said that Rowan had been in Court that morning but he was not really fit to appear end was being kept n inmate at the Inflrmery so to Le away from certain temptations. ;Sir. Steel said he represented Cheaters end had no objection to a remand. Prisoner had been liberated on a recognisance of surety,butas be was a householder, be asked that he might be remanded on his On .1 re 3og- nisances. The magistrates agreed to this and the case was accordingly remanded for a week. ALLEGED THEFT OF MONEY. PRISONER REMANDED.

At the Borough Polies Court, on Wednesday, George Marston, a well-dressed man was remanded on two charges, one of stealing from the shop counter of 27, Pinner's Brow, a purse containing 25., the property of Ellen Marrow, and also with peddling on the same day without a licence. It transpired that the prisoner went into the prosecutrix's shop and sold her one of a number of mantles which .he was p3diling. Mrs. Marrow left her purse contain- ing 2s. on the counter, and on prisoner leaving the purse was missed. Shortly afterwards the licensee of the Glassmaker's Arms, Fennel-street, was in his yard when the empty purse was thrown over, and on going out saw the prisoner walking away. He was afterwards appre- hended. Prisoner said he gave way to a sadden tampta- tion.—Prisoner was brought up yesterday. A written statement from prisoner was read which said that on entering the shop the purse was lying in front of him and he took it on the impulse of the moment. Tbere was no meditation whatsoever. With reference to the licence he said he did not know he was doing any s eong.

—lnspector Williamson said the prisone-r bad bee-n fent mead to three months for a cheque fraud at Birmingham. Prisoner said he was drawn into the bother by another man who got 18 month.. Prisoner wts sentenced to ten days' imprisonment. "MIN amnia
