div.head: AN UNWELCOME VISITOR AT ORFORD.
div.p: AN UNWELCOME VISITOR AT ORFORD.

At the Warrington Occasional Court, yesterday,before Colonel Buckton, Thomas Henry Jefferies, a youth, of Wellfield-street, Warrington, was charged with being found in a dwelling-house in the occupation of Ralph Lawton, Orford, on Thursday, for an unlawful purpose. —Annie Lawton, thughter of Ralph Lawton, Brookside Farm, Orford, said she was upstairs at three o'clock on Thursday afternoon when she heard a noise on the stairs, so she came down. She then saw prisoner who asked for some bread. She gave him same bread and

butter. She did not see him inside the house, but she knew it could Inve been nobody else but bitr. Tne door tug open. She saw him twenty minutes after- wards in the lane.—P.C. Woolf said that from informa- tion received he went in search of prisoner and found him hiding under soma bushes.—Mr. Jefferies char- scterised his son as an idle fellow and a terrible liar.— On prisoner prom'sing to work end be a good lad, the case was dismissed with a caution.

div.head: Warrington Borough Court.
div.p: Warrington Borough Court.
MONDAY.—Before Alderman Smethurst (chairmln), Alderman J. Evans and "Messrs. S. Wright, W.Roberts, and G. Piling. _ _

A VIOLENT PRISONER.—WiIIiam Jones of Cloth Hall yard was charged with haying been found on the enclosed premises of the London and North-Western Railway sidings at Arpley on Saturday last, for an unlawful purpose and with intent to commit a felony; further with using obscene language in Wilson Patten- street, and also with using threats to Detective Ernest Clerk, of the London and North-Western Railway Company.—Detectice Clark stated that about 10.30 p.m. on Saturday he was on duty in Arpley when he saw the prisoner walking about on the metals. Witness went to him and asked him what be aas doing there. Prisoner wanted to know who witness was and dared him to lay hands upon him. iVitneas told prisoner that he had better go to the Police Station with him. Prisoner then said he would murder witness if he touched him. He thee started to struggle and after a while witness became winded and shouted for assistance. A man named Durham then went to his assistance. Prisoner said he would put his knife through witness if he could get it out. At the Police Station he aglin threatened witness and said that if be got time for that job ho would do for him afterwards. Joseph Durham, a pit boy. employed at Collins Green, said he was in Arpley on the Saturday night when he heard Clark shout for rissistanee. He went to Clark's assistance 2nd helped him to get prisoner to the Police Station. Witness corroborated Clark's statements as to prisoner's threats towards him.—The Coairman said the charge was a very serious one. Referring to the threats he said that prisoner seemed to have no guard upon his language when be was drunk. The bench would however take a len'ent view of the ca3e as it Was his first offence and fine him ss. or seven days'.—The Chairman thanked Durham for his assistance to the police and said they were extremely obliged to him. Continuing, he said that perhaps only for his timely as,istance the charge might have been a worse one. Inspector Williamson said they were in receipt of a letter from the railway authorities saying they were going to reward Durham for his assistance. TRAM-DRI V F:R AND CONDUCTOR ASSAULTED.— William Feeney, is young man living in Ellen-street,was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Manchester-road the previous night; further with assaulting Joseph Clarke, tram-driver, and John Henry Cook, a tram conductor, on the same date.—John Henry Cook, a conductor, of 14, Cuaaberland-street, said that about 8 40 tbe previous night be was on his tram at the Nfanchest 3r-road terminus. He there saw the prisoner, with another man, kick a boy named Percy Duckworth. Witness jumped off his car and told prisoner that was no way to chastise a youth. Prisoner thereupon struck witness in the chest. The prisoner's companion then told witness he wanted to speak to hire. Driver Clarke then followed and while there the prisoner went apto him and struck him a deliberate blow on the nose. He also used very bad language. Constable Steele then came up and took prisoner into charge. Prisoner was not drunk and knew what he was doing.—P.C. Steele spoke to arresting the prisoner.—Prisoner was fined in the costs (14s. 6d.) OBST Itt7CTlON.—James Bridge, 2, New-road, WAS charged with unlawfully obstructing Lyme-street on the 14th August.—He pleaded not guilty.—The evidence showed that about 10.30 on Saturday night a constable saw defendant with a meat truck in Lyme-street. He stood there from 10.30 until 10.45. The constable went to him end told him he was causing an obstruction, the road being impassable. Defendant moved about two yards and on being told again moved another two yards. The Constable then told him that he had better get out of the street altogether. About eleven o'clock the constable returned to Lyme-street, and saw the defend- ant there again. He stood from 11 o'clock to a quarter past 11 in the same spot.—Defendant attempted to prove that he did move out of Lyme-street into Peter- street.—ln answer to the Bench, the Constable ssid the road was impassable, the defendant standing in the very narrow part. He seemed persistent in his obstruction. —Defendant denied that he was soliciting orders.—The Constable: He wis shouting IA. lb. meat. (Laughter.) Sergeant Cooper corroborated the constable's state- ments.—A fine of ss. 6d. was imposed. LAMP-SM ASHING.—Thomas lieaney,a youth, 8, Ellen- street,was charged with breaking the glass of a street i lamp n Ellen-street on the 26th of July.—Thomas Johnson, a boy, said he saw the defendant deliberately throws, duck stone at the lamp and break the glass and the mantle. It was not done by accident.—A Corpora- tion official from the Gas Department said that rep airs to lamps each year in Warrington cost £l5O. This particular lamp had been broken five times. on June 19tb, July 9th, July 26th and July 31st. The total number of lamps broken in the year were 2,044 and mantles 2,BlB.—Defendant was warned and ordered to pay 10s. • DRI:NK n CllAßGE.—Thomas Cook, a carter, of 36, ()afraid-street, was fined 10s. for being drunk in charge of a horse and lurry on Chester-road.
FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Smethurst (chairmail), Councillor Wilkinson, and Messrs. A. J.

Jolley, W. Furness, H. Thornton, and G. Pilling. A WIFE SEEKS SEPARATION.—Peter Newton,Harciy-st., was summoned by his wife (Ada) for persistent cruelty, whereby she asked for a separation order.—Defendant pleaded not guilty.—Complainant stated that a fort- night last Monday night he was worse for drink and met her outside. He hit her and said that if he could get her home he would brain her. The next morning he would nut go to wok. In the afternoon he went to complainant's mother and made her pawn his vest for drink.oa the followingThursdly he hit complainant in the eye and blacked it while she had the baby in her arms and Mao kicked her up and down the house. She had been married two years last Christmas, and he bad been away fram her one'. They had two children. •He had heea hitting her ever since they were married.—Defendant said his wife had run him in debt—A separation order was granted, allowing the wife 10s. per week. FALSE ATTESTATION.—WiIIiaUI Green was charged with making a false answer when enlisting in the King's Liverpool Regiment at Warrington on the 2:1n1 Nlay.—Chief Inspect.,r Williamson said that tl-H prisoner had been received into custody from the military authorities. The charge was of making a false answer when enli,ting by saying that he had not served iu the Army or Navy before, but it was ascertained that he had teen in the Navy and wasdismisserl front the service fora naval offence.—Prisoner was sentenced to one month's imprisonment. A NAVAL DESERTER.—WiIIiam Georgb Fox Was charged with being a &sorter from H.M.S. Acehron stationed at Chatham since 1903.—Inspector Williamson said that prisoner was arrested the previeas day by Sergeant Meacock and PC. Holland. The naval authorities had been communicated with but no reply bad come. They were however expecting an answer that thy; he therefore asked for a remand.—The prisoner will be handed over to the military authorities to-morrow.

ASSAULT OR FIGHTING ?—John Mithr of Ellen-street was summonei by Joseph Graham Albert-st., for unlaw- full assault by beating and kicking him on the 24th August. Defendant who was represented by Mr.T.S.Steel pleaded "not g uilty."—Graham Watedthat on Tuesday night at a quarter past eleven o'clock he was going horne along Bewsey-road. He was walking behind defendant. On getting to Bewsey Bridge the defendvt turned round and gave complainant a push in the mouth and started kicking him all over the road. A companion named Isaac Horton pulled defendant off bim.:—Defeni- ant then slunk away " like a dog."—Mr. Steel for the defence pointed out that complainant used very bad language and deserved the thrashing he got. Com- plainant showed fight and if he had come off the conqueror they wonid have heard nothing about the case. evidence having been given the bench imposel as fine of 10s. and costs (215.) . THREATS TO A WIFF..—John Thomas Timmis,Aitken-st., was summoned by his wife for threats whereby she was afraid be would do her some bodily injury. She stated that he ran after her in the street on the 22nd cf August and threatened to murder her and she was afraid to live with him.Last,Friday night he went to the Hippodrome and took the children and while there he got turned out for fighting and left the children there. Ihey had to be brought home by a friend. He would not give her any of his money and he expected the home to be keep going w:thout money.—After being entreated by the chairman to give up drink and be united with his wife defendant said he would try and he case was dismissed.

div.head: Occasional Court.
div.p: Occasional Court.

A SUSPICIOUS VlStTon.—At the Warrington Occasional Court, on Monday, before Mr. F. A. Frost, Sidney Sueath, win said he came from Sunderland, was charged with having been suspected of loitering with intent to commit a felony at Stockton Heath, on the previous day. Prisoner pleaded not guilty.,--;4lr. Thomas F. W. Dixon, Ferndale, Grappenhall-road, Stockton Heath, said the prisoner called at his house on Friday night, but witness did not see him. Witnesk was at home on Sunday afternoon and the prisoner was pointed out to him. He was then acting in a suspicioas manner. Witness watched him for some time, and atw prisoner call at Mr. Conuor's house, where he stayed for some time. He then went further along the road in the direction of Grappenhall. Anen anyone went along the road he pretended to be making notes on paper. Witness was talking to a friend and prisoner inquired where Mr. Grocott lived. Prisoner was told that he was away and he then asked when he would be bank. They could not tell him. He asked how long Mr. Groeott had been away and then went out of the dis- trict.—Sergeant Barlow said that he saw prisoner at about quarter past five. When asked„prisoner refused to give any account of himself. He told witness that his name was Sneath. Witness took him to the Stockton Heath Police Station.—Prisoner said that he came from Sanderland, and that he had come over to see an old friend at Stockton Heath.—The Chairman said he was c3nvinced that prisoner was acting in a suspicious manner. Prisoner did not seem to give a satisfactory account of himself. He would be finod 10s. or seven day's imprisonment.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

The weekly meeting of this Society on Sunday was well attended, the chair being occupied by Mr. D. Owyn. An address on "Running the Rice "was given by Mr. H. Woolley, who pointed out that a runner before entering the race always wanted to know the conditions and to see the course. So it was on the Christian race course. The runner also cast off everything which hindered speed, and in the same way professing Christ:ans were sometimes hindered by little besetting sins, which should first of all be cast off. Mr. J. Cooper read the lesson and Mr. 41. Healey led the prayer. Miss Silcock sang sweetly" Nearer my God to Thee" Mr. Pluton Mus. Bac. presided at the organ. .
the Secretary reported on the illness of Bro. Grosty and gave strong hopes of b's speedy recovery. He els, proposed that a mess tge of sympathy be sent him at the hospital, which was agreed to.

div.head: Baptist Church, Golhorne-street.
div.p: Baptist Church, Golhorne-street.

On Sunday evening the Rev. R. E. L3tharen con- tinued his series of addre.tsas on the " Angelus " the subject being the "Gospel of worship." His text was taken from Zechariah xiv., 20, "In that day there shall be upon the bells of the houses, 110 l iness unto the Lord:" Referring to the picture he said that though the church was in the background of it, it made its influence felt in the fl;ures that filled the foreground. They were not in the church but what the church stood for was in them and so even in their work they were worshippers, The influence of religion only begins when it overflows the church and passes into the streets and fialds and houses where men and women live and love and labour. The measure of a man's religion is his nrectical esti- mate of what God is worth to him. God's" worth- ship "to a man—that is his worship. It is not enough to believe in a God. The important thing is what God you believe in. It is God as revealed by Jesus as a gracious leather who alone can become near and real so as tn Ibe the one grand reality of life. Referring to the two figures in the picture with their heads bowed in prayer, Mr. Let'aeren said that it was in prayer that worship found its most natural expression. The best humsn analogy of prayer was not presentine petitions to a Sovereign but intercourse with a Fried, so that prayer comes to be a constant sense of God and the reference of all life's circumstances to their centre in God's will. The great rafeguird and opportunity of worship is the Sabbath. It stmis for the rights of God and the soul; but not less for the rights of the body and the poor. To destroy man's respect for the Sabbath is to open the flood gates of peril. You cal% play fast and loose with God's laws and get off scot free. By these thoughts their minds were led to what was the supreme spiritual message of this great picture the wedding of work with worship the true bridal of the earth and sky. Mr. Letheren illustrated this with a sketch of the life of Bcother Lawrence the author of "The Practice of the Presence of God "—a book that is one of the half-dozen spiritual masterpieces of the world and was the work of a cook in the kitchen. The text was an enticipation of the time when the abolition of the distinction between things secular and snored should be an accom- plished fact and all the bells of life ring in harmony with God's holy will.

div.head: MILLION ANCESTORS.
div.p: A MILLION ANCESTORS.

I asked a friend a short time back how many ancestors he had in the direct line twenty generations back. After a minute's reflection he suggested fifty. It may be a little surprising and of interest to same of your readers to learn that they each have had more than a million ancestors within comparatively recent years, and that without taking into account uncles and aunts. Starting with one's parents, each person usually has two, a father and a mother. The father had his two parents and the motberlad hers. Thus each person had four grandparents. One step farther and we have eight great-grandparents. I know a case within living memory where a man has fbur great-gnindparta.ts all living. A simple calculation gives the tistonithing result that our lineal ancestors during twenty generations number no fewer than 1,018,576, as shown below, or sufficient people if all living to populate the whole of Wales. div.head: CaICKETING BROTHERS.
div.p: CaICKETING BROTHERS.

In an interesting anecdotal article on Brothers of the Cricket Field" which appears in the September "Windsor Magazine,"accompanied izry many portraits, Sir Home Gordon, Bart., writes : "Then there were the Steels; who all hailed from Liverpool. I met Douglas once in Kerry, and against an eleven of Tralee be made more runs than all the opposing eleven, bowled most of them out, and kept wicket at the end at which he was bowling. A. G.' of that ilk was so great a cricketer that to praise him would be superfluous. H. B.' was a powerful hitter who never obtained his Blue' at Cambridge' and E. E.'—who boseled not many seasons back for the Gentlemen at the Oval—still goes annually on a tour against the public schools. - "Always associated with the Steels will be the Studds, another family splendid in every respect. Three attained distinction in the game. Mr. J. E. K., though never so good as the other two, was a capital run-getter, and is now the moving spirit of that great Institution, the Polytechnic. Mr. G. B. was a really beautiful bat to watch, and so good a field that his occasional uncertainty in holding a catch was positively disconcerting. The finest was Mr. C. T. Studd, who cut short his career in the field in order to become a missionary in China. He was a very good bat and a capital slow bowler, as typical an Eton cricketer as one could wish to point out. Mr. 11. W. Studd, who went into the Guards, would have been quite good enough to have bowled for his Uuiversity had he gone up." The September Windsor Magazine is a notable holiday number, full of flue stories by leading novelists, and articles instructive and entertaining, lavishly illustrated ' throughout. Complete stories by Justus Miles Forman, Barry Pain, Florence Warden, Charles G. D. Roberts, Kate Jordan, and other distinguished authors are included, in addition to a long instalment of Max Pemberton's picturesque new serial, "White Wall." Fifteen of Mr. George Hitchcock's beautiful pictures of sacred themes, and the more modern flower fields of Holland, which the artist has made his own, are finely reproduced with a biographical article; and the second paper in the important series on the Canals of Great Britain carries a number of interesting illustrations. No dog lover should miss sixtem plates selected from Maud Earl's famous painting of dog life and character, the set being drawn from the group known as "Terriers and Toys."

div.head: POLICE SPORTS.
div.p: THE POLICE SPORTS.
A Grand Success.

Aided by fair weather and a capital entry the annual sports organised by the Borough Police Force, which were held on the Warrington Football ground, Wilderspool-road, on Thursday afternoon, were a com- plete success. The local custodians of the peace are always ready to give a helping hand to any deserving local charities, and the large crowd which was present testified to their excellent work. Referring to the entries, many noted athletes were present, including some Olympia champions. C. Berry, the local crack cyclist, and Sherratt, of Wigan took part in the cycle races. B. W, Pankhurst, the well-known all round athlete,also competed. There was a grand entry for the 100 yards flat race handicap which neccessitated it being run off in 10 heats. In the final V. Bell, of Peover, won a Well- earned first doing the distance in 10 2-ssec. and J. Leather, of Latchford was a good. second. Some excellent cycling was witnessed in the two miles bicycle hlndicap, J. Rogerson, of Wigan, proving the winner.J.Hands,of Warrington,also proved himself of no mean ability and arrived half a wheel behind Rogerson. i \V. Green of Warrington was very prominent n the 220 yards flat race (open). After winning his heat in splendid style, he breasted the tape first in the final, J. j. Brabazon of Cunliffe being second. In the one mile bicycle handicap (open), C. Berry, of Warrington, who was put near scratch was unable to win his heat. In the final J. Clare, of Leigh, proved the winner by a machine length. The local police made a fine show of sprinting in the 100 yards flat race handicap. J. Glover proved the fleetest, H. Armstrong being second, IL Wood- land third and H. Woollacot fourth. Much interest was centred in the half-mile flat race handicap, the winner being A. Pritchard of Chester, C. W. Hunt of Crosfield's R.C. being a good second. Pritchard was also successful in the one mile flat race handicap and carried off first prize, A ,Parkinson of Liverpool was second and A. Hall of Chester being third. During the afternoon a military tournament was provided by a contingent of privates from the barracks under the direction of Sergeant-Major Scott and Sergeant Knight. The Warrington Blue Coat School Band, also pro- vided a capital programme of music. Thanks are due to the officials, whose indefatigable efforts resulted in the programme being carried through without a hitch.
At—the close of the proceedings Miss Forsbaw distributed the prizes to the winners.

div.head: LATE MRS. ELINOR HOLrdES.
div.p: THE LATE MRS. ELINOR HOLrdES.

As previously announced in oar obituary columa there passed away at Rougemont, Great Sankey, 03 Wednesday the 18th inst. Mrs. Elinor Holmes, widow of the late Charles John Holmes, agod'Bs years. lie' bright and chatty companionship was much sought -afie.r by numerous friends and acquaintances in all condi- tions of life, especially during the past few years when she was more or less confined in doors. faculties were bright and active to the last and she toel. a keen interest in the affairs of the outer world. T 0 the members of her own family she could relate interesting narratives of her younger days, o.ftert repeating poeiky some of which was quite original- On her 85th birthday (7th July) she wrote letters te her friends and was apparently in the best of health. She seemed to feel the hot weather, however, of last week from which she did not recover, and so witheu" any pain or suffering she simply ceased t-.) breathe. The interment took place at the well,kept quiet, an retired burial ground of the Society of Friends.at Penketh on Saturday afternoon. last. As an evideal of the love that was felt for her by many people, 110.3- respect by others, a very large number assembled the graveside. Mr. Joseph Walker, of Eccl IA es, alluded to the appropriateness of the test which was on the memorkal card "Blessed arwthe pare in heart for they shall see God" and went on to remark that she was now laid beside her partner who haa spent so much time in the public service, and w.ho, whether amid tokens of approval on the stern winds of criticism, was at any rate sure of a haven of rest and comfort on his return home. In the meeting house afterwards Mrs. Garnett,Penketh,spoke on behalf of the Warrington Branch of British Women's Temperair/ Association, and said that at the very earnest desire of that body Mrs. Holmes accepted .the presidency fer a time, and although she was never able to attend far of its meetings or gatherings .she always cheerful-12r subscribed to the funds for carrying on the IrOr,!;.: After a few appropriate remarks from Mr. JC!,..L"' Ashworth and Mr. William Nash (Manchester), Pie meeting was brought to a conclusion.

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

Considerable interest is shown this week the performance given by the Eight Lancashire Lacig; They are a youthful, well-turned-out companY, au!' earn enthusiastic plaudits by the cleverness of thelc dancing. Smart footwork always meets with due appreciation, and some of the" lads could coinPeT with the best in the profession and not be shainea" in 'kiddie. Yetta varies the usual tight-wire-performan by dancing to the orchestral music. Her steps ale` gracefully performed, and demonstrate the lady to be, an expert on the wire. Billie Burford has recorder. an immense success with her musical monologue auu songs. She has a style of her own, and render! "Knock three times at the front street door" with point and expression which bring down the! house. Bernard and Weston are a pair 11 funny men who have been seen here before. 3lue,, of their business is new, and there wa doubt about the success of their efforts to amuse. Milsted Bell Trio present a very lively sketch entitlet& "Three sharps in a Flat," which does not drag for 3 single second. The " slavey " in the princess robot does weird things with the train, and provokes y°?. of the laughter. The four Sidney girls give -a brigr.,; turn as vocalists and skipping rope dancers, and Os Warner, soubrette, sings nicely. One of the succe_s.se of the evening-however, is undoubtedly Walter Bing' a humourist whom we do not remember to have sfe3 before. Ho had the audience in a roar all the tone he was on, and his drolleries were all the more efit_e;:, tive when uttered in a tearful sort of voice incape"'" of imitation. Quite a sensation is caused by the Palace pictures, illustrating "The Fear," a gruesoule/ tragedy acted by the French.

div.head: WOES OF THE NOBLEMAN.
div.p: WOES OF THE NOBLEMAN.

How the Outcry has Helped the Budget. "The outcry about the troubles of noblemen has dose a great deal to open the eyes of the English peoPle tc! the real nature of the Budget," said Mr. J. M. Robert son, M.P., at the. Sun Ball, Bootle, on Wednesdal evening. The Dukes threatened Co make up for their increasel taxation by retrenching in their charities. Well, the?! gentlemen are very much mis.a ken if they think tP.,if nation is going to let the po3r starve if they stop their charities. If any new poverty should be produced bit the Budget, the State will undertaite to see to tha_ poverty, and, if necessary, further tax these gentler:nal' to do it. (Applause). "After this Budget has been passed, I think thae millionaires will find that England is still a very g",„ country for millionaires, and we hope that for the P") it will be a rather better country to live in. Mystery, however, surrounds the shooting of the latter beast. The shooting of the 90cer05, a huge bull, was a feat, according to a New York correspondent, "such as na Af r ican hunter has ever exceed( d." Mr. Roosevelt's son, Kermit, has shot the largest lion °f the whole bag. 3 Our photograph shows the ex-President and his son (in light suits) at the t aces held at Nairobi, British East Africa.

SANDBACH AND ABBEY FIELD.

The journey deserved much more time than we were able to give. A full day would not have been too much, but owing to bad management we are not able to make the early start we have planned and as a sub- ditute take a convenient lift on the railway. Winsford is our alighting place, and with a generous afternoon before us we begin the journey. Guided by the pillar of smoke that rises above it we find Middlewich, and paus- ing only to make the acquaintance of its old church and monuments, take the level road that skirts the Trent and Mersey Canal. The cyclist who has time will take the road that leads through Occleston Green or the furthei )ne that takes him past the gates of Bradwall Flail, but we have much to do and follow the luickest and easiest road.

div.head: SANDBAOIi.
div.p: SANDBAOIi.

Sandbach will impress the visitor as th( ideal of a Cheshire market town. It s ifficiently modern to be scrupulously clean, it has some neat buildings, it is sufficiently r33tful—even though it is market day—to s )othe the most tender nerves, it is age-toned and has some glorious memorials of the past. It is these antiquarian objects that the pilgrim will want to understand and we must give all the space we can allow him to an elucidation of their mysteries. He will look

div.head: e''lP••%,.§
div.p: ANCIENT CROSSES, SANDBACH.

)n the ancient Crosses as pilgrims have done br ages, and may be tempted into specula- tions—as most other pilgrims have been—as ,o their weird and impressive carvings. But et him beware of asking the opinion of a gative. Truth to tell these shapes in stone have puzzled the wisest heads and it is hardly -o be expected that they will yield their 3ecrets to the man in the Market place.

div.head: ANCIENT SAXON CROSSES.
div.p: THE ANCIENT SAXON CROSSES.

The two ancient crosses are the glory of iandbach and its peculiar pride. They lift ;heir heads calmly over the market place as ;hey have done for a full milennium, and 103 k down with some suspicion of scorn upon the poor creature of a day that comes with sketch book or camera. For the learned tntiquarian they may show a touch of pity, but take them for all in all they are as inscrutable as the Sphinx. _ _ _

It is fitting that We have come on pilgrim- age here, for the crosses have been the goal of genuine pilgrimages for centuries, and thousands have knelt here as on sacred ground and expecting a blessing as their reward. And in modern centuries the spot has drawn every famous antiquary our country has produced to add to rest his theory of the meaning of the ancient shrine. We must try to make the better acquaintance of the old pillars of stone. The cpmmon belief is that they were 3rected to mark the place where Christianity was first preached in the kingdom of Mercia. This broad kingdom,as everyone knows,came up to Lancashire and it is quite possible that the prevailing tradition is correct. But we are not beholding the crosses as pious hands., iet them up twelve hundred years ago. En the sixteenth or seventeenth century they were thrown down, possibly under the order Elizabeth against superstitious images, or possibly during the Civil War, and it was not for a long time that people woke up to their interest. Then began the search for fragments. It was found that the top of the smaller cross was in use as the door step a cottage, other parts had been laid as pavement, and one large piece is known to lie under the foundations of a house. Other portions adorned rockeries, and the base of the great cross had been placed across the town well. The main parts of this cross came into the hands of Sir John Crewe, a zealous Protestant. He liked the carvings, but as one of them was a crucifix he care- fully covered it with mortar before setting up the stone in his ground. Little by little the pieces were returned, and as many as could be obtained were joined together. But alas, they are fat from their original glory. It is estimated that the large cross must have raised its head twenty-five feet above the ground. The fragments only reach a height of seventeen feet and the smaller cross
is only twelve. They originally -1;a71 circular heads but these are gone, and the old battered pillars we see to-day give but the faintest knowledge of the glories that were.

div.head: ANCIENT CHRISTIAN SCULPTURES.
div.p: ANCIENT CHRISTIAN SCULPTURES.

But there is enough to fascinate. The large cross portrays some scenes in the life of Christ as they appealed to the artist of twelve centuries ago. In the centre is the crucified Christ, and around him the four Evangelists and their emblems. Above them is a figure with head down- wards—probably a commemoration of the traditional crucifixion of Peter. Below the crucifix is the scene of the Nativity with quaint animals looking into the manger. Lower still is a figure surmounted by a dove and a possible carving of Peter with the keys, and in a circle three figures, two doing obeisance to the centre one. On the north side eleven apostles are to be counted, and above a flying monster with a terrible cloven tongue is apparently' breathing on them. On the west side are eight double compartments. The first part is filled by dragons with con- torted wings. A winged and sitting figure above probably represent the appearing of the Angel to Zachary in the Temple. Above, Simon bears the cross, and in a higher panel the Saviour, distinguished by a mark around his head, is led bound by a rope. The smaller cross does not yield -so easily to our efforts at decipherntent. Twelve figures suggest twelve apostles and there are figures that may stand for the Trinity. The circular tops have been filled in by figures that were placed like the spokes of a wheel and traces of these remain. But there is much left for the future antiquarian and we leave feeling that we have done little to unravel

the history that is written in such cryptic forms upon these strange old stones. A point which none of the antiquaries seem to have noted is that these two crosses appear to have been of exactly the same size and shape as two that stood over the reputed grave of Arthur on the isle of Avalon. Who knows, then, but that they may cover the bones of some Saxon hero—some St. Oswald of long ago whose memorial has outlived his memory.

div.head: OLD HALL.
div.p: THE OLD HALL.
Sandbach can boast at least two really fine timbered buildings. One of them "The Old Bear" we inspect—from without of course— and pass to give a more detailed survey to the " Old Hall."

There is a wealth of beauty and interest in this fine old Cheshire home, though curiously enough, nobody seems to know anything of its history. The surrounding water suggests that it was once a moated Hall or Manor house and it may have suc- ceeded a fortress placed here on the high bank. But in the absence of records we can only take things as they are and study to our antiquarian delight the fine old hall. Beautiful fire places of carved and panelled oak adorn the chief rooms, the one upstairs being especially good, and at the top of the stairs is a rare appendage, a dog gate, designed to keep the dogs from wandering upstairs. These old gates were once very common, but exceedingly few have survived. We cannot help noting that the gate is strong enough and high enough to prevent dogs of any size whether four or two legged getting into forbidden places.

div.head: ABBEY FIELD.
div.p: ABBEY FIELD.

But we have promised ourselves yet another little treat whilst we are out on wheel to-day. We are going to ask per- mission to explore the old park and Hall of A.bbeyfield. In pre-Reformation times Abbot's Field, as it was then called, was owned by the Abbot of Dienlacres. A small island in the lake contains all that is left of the first building and as we have no boat we are not able to explore them. The present Hall has been variously patched and its appearance does not suggest its antiquity. We find it, to our regret, empty, and shorn of much of its interest and homeliness.
We are allowed, however to walk through its fine rooms and we bestow our admiration upon the oak-panelled hall and IF raceful staircase, • A REAL COCK-PIT.

We ascend the stair to examine a chamber such as must be rare in this virtuous age— a real cock-pit. It seems that the dining room was considered to be too low and the owner decided to raise the ceiling. In doing this he quite spoiled the room above, leaving it with a height of only five feet or there- abouts. The chamber became in this way mOre or less hidden from view, and as men, though they could not stand, could com- fortably sit in the ample room, it commended itself as an admirable place for cqck-fighting, and we are told that the premises sheltered some very fine samples of game cocks, who were brought out to amuse and excite the gentlemen of Cheshire.

We are glad to creep out of the cribbed and stuffy cockpit and get to the park, wondering meanwhile why men with spread- ing acres to feast their eyes and souls upon should crawl to an attic to watch the piteous bloodshed of a cock fight. My friend, to whom I unbosom myself, suggests that it is a sure proof of the exist- ence of a devil and that I may get some good theology out of it. And I am half inclined to agree.
We have certainly found something to think about as we traverse the road that leads us to home. A.M.

div.head: iscELLANY.
div.p: iscELLANY.

Our" Pilgrimage" articles have brought us a sheaf of comments, chiefly enthusiastic appreciations,for which we tender our thanks. One of our readers is disposed to be very sarcastic at the expense of the rhyming Squire who exhorts men to slay the "dragon drunkenness" by rebuilding beautifying and making attractive the public house of that name. We have nothing to do with the aptitude of the Squire's rhymes. It certainly does seem an incongruity to place them where they are. For ourselves we should have put the verse over the village pump. a ** * *

Another who followed in our footsteps wants to know the meaning of the public house sign in Comberba,ch "The Weaver and Burgamot." Burgamot should be written Bergamot. It is the name of the Italian town at which a kind of coarse tapestry was first manufactured. The name of the town was transferred to the article.
Yet another quotes for us a rhyming sign post " one of the best."
Trespassers this notice heed Onward you may not proceed Unless to 'Arley Hall you speed an suggests that the same rhymster must have given its motto to the inn at Appleton Thorn
You may safely while sober sit under the thorn But if drunk overnight it will prick you next morn ** * *

Another reader delighted at the prospect of knowing more of his native county wants us to give him a chapter on Nixon, the Cheshire prophet, and his strange predictions. This we will do right gladly if our corres- pondent can give patience for a week or two.

FEEDING DOGS.

As a rule, two n7te-ai-s-a-cia; s-ufli-c-efor an adult dog, says" Fancier," in" Farm and Home." A light break- fast and a good meal at night—excepting in the case of watchdogs, when the animal should be given at mid-day and not at night, so as to keep them on the alert. There are, however, many successful exhibitors and breeders who feed their dogs only once a day. We made inquiries at a large show some 'few weeks back, and found that a bulldog, collie, Irish terrier, and wolf- hound, all of whom took first prizes, were only fed once a day (at night), and the meal consisted of raw meat, varied at times with vegetables soaked in gravy or biscuits. The quantity of food to be given varies with the breed, size and condition, but as a rule, a dog in good health requires about A. to ozs. of solid food per day for every pound he weighs. Liquid food, such as milk, gravy, eta. are not included in Ulla table.

div.head: BACKING THE BUDGET.
div.p: BACKING THE BUDGET.
ANOTHER SUCCESSFUL OPEN-MR MEETING

Another open-air meeting under the auspices' of the Warrington Progre,sive Labour League was held on Monday evening. There was a large attendance despite the inclement weather. Mr. J. C. Holland took the chair and supporting him on the lurry, which served as a platform, were Cbuncillor James Kendall, J.P., of Manchester, Mess's. E. Wynne Jones, J. A. J. Morton and Joseph Howes, jun. The CHAIRMAN said there was one question that was burning itself out and was sinking into oblh ion and that was Tariff Reform. The speaker referred to Sir Charles E. Sdiwaim's letter to the " Manchester Guardian "a few eays ago in which he stated : "When we consider that in 1907 our total trade reached £980,137,000 imports and exports added together, and that with our population of only some forty millions the trade of tho United Kingdom amounted to nearly £220,C00,000 more than that of Germany—whose trade exceeded that of the United *tates—the former of which has at least half as many more inhabitants, and the latter nation double as many as ourselves, we shall do well to have a little patience, and not dream of adopting quack ren edies like Protection or Tariff Reform, which only means increased pr.; ees of food and other commodi.tie7. Unemployment is badtbut in protected America it is far worse, as the United I &rites official statistics show." Concluding tbe Chair- man asked them to support Free Trade and the Budget. Liberalism meant an untaxed loaf, and opportunities for all. Toryism meant dear food and dear goods. Councillor KENDALL, who is a very entertaining speaker, then addressed the meeting. De said in the political history of England no Budget had ever required to receive the same discussion as that had. It was a most remarkable thing that in the history of politics a political party had dared to take to the people of this country its financial proposals. It was a significant fact that it had been reserved for a Liberal Govern- ment—in his opinion the finest Government they had ever bad—(hear, hear)—to bring their Budget proposals and put them before the people who would.have to pay the taxes, and challenge criticism and comment. There had not, been many Budgets that bad been worth it, except perhaps Sir William Harcourt's, the one which Included death duties. They were grumbling at the death duties. He wished they would defer his taxes until he was dead. (Laughter.) The Budget contained three main principles. The first one was that it put I taxation on the best able to bear it. (Applause) That meant th it those who had most should pay most, and those who had least should pay least, The second principle was, that in order to raise the requisite money fer the carrying on of the Government in this country it was time to look round and see if there were anything that was untaxed that could be taxed. That was a sensible arrangement, wasn't it? (Voices: Aye!) If they had allowed splendid fields of taxation to go untaxed there was no earthly reason why they should not tax them now. The third principle was that everbody should contribute something. Surely that was a fair and reasonable proposition. When the Bodget came out there was a huge hullabaloo. The Tory party immediately began to look up the dictionary and fished out the words, "robbery, spoliation, con- fiscation" and all sorts of "ations." They had bad the wonderful spectacle of poor, downtrodden millionaires —(laughter)—who had gone around trying to get up leagues and organisations and had been asking working- men to help them to keep their money: (Laughter). Fancy the millionaire asking them to join his league and give their subscriptions towards fighting his battle, because a far too long delayed tax had been put upon him. They bad not responded to the appeal of the landlord and soon they would be coming round and telling them they were unkind, and unsympathetic. (Laughter). They would wonder how it was that they did not get excited and raise an outcry because the landowners were going to be taxed. Continuing the speaker said that there was no need to worry,the Budget would 'go through. (Applause). The House of Lords had not got much sense, but they had got a little. We were not going to have a general election over the Budget. Only last week they bad Mr. Lyttelton claiming the Budget as theirs, so they were not going to throw it out, if it were theirs. The Tories said they now did not find so much fault with the Budget because they had hammered it into shape. He thought the electors, who had teen appealed to all over the country had hammered the Tory party out of shape—(laughter)—and the result was that the Budget wasnow receiving the benediction of those who had tried to thwart it. Continuing, lie said that there was to be an increase in the tobacco tax. He was going to deal with that because he was fond of a pipe of tobacco. Instead of paying 3d. for an ounce of thick twist they would now have to pay 31d. What a terrible thing! (Laughter.) There was also to be an increase in the spi?it duty of 3s. 9d. per gallon,which was going to bring in close on two millions of money. Then there was going to be a further increase under the head of increase of licences that was going to bring in about 21 millions. So that those who smoked and those who drank spirits were going to con- tribute a little bit towards the old age pensions, which had been granted by the present Government— (applause)—and towards making this country safe for their wives and families. Why had not workingmen formed their leagues ? Because they had too much pride and self-respect; because they were too patriotic ; because they knew they wee going to have old age pensions, social reforms and the best fleet in the world. Referring to the licence duties he said that perhaps some of them were fend of a pint of beer. Beer was not touched in that Budget, and if their local publicans had put up the price be ad v ieed them. to go to a cheaper shop. The publicans were"having"them. "Don't you be had." (Laughter). In London the brewer had raised the price of beer 12s. a barrel ; and yet the tax worked out only 3d.a barrelahad been proved in a court of law that the average profit on a barrel of beer was 14s. 6d. Me ventured to think that en extra tax of 3d. would not do them very much harm. (Laughter and applause). The new tax would bring in abolit 4 millions and the brewers were trying to get 20 millions from the people of this country. But it was not working! He believed that to some extent the tax would result in temperance. Proceeding be said that anything that tended to check the national drink bill was a national good. Be said that as a citizen and not as a teetotaler, for he. was not one. Any thing that curbed the appetite of drink was good for the country as a whole,good for the children, wife and husband. The more sober husbands and moderate husbands there were the better it would be. If it; were going to help forward the temperance movement and reduce the national drink bill they had a right to support the Budget. (Applause). As long as the country had a national thirst, there would still be enough for the brewers. Proceeding to explain the income tax section of the Budget, Councillor Kendal said that under a Liberal Government for. the first time in this country a difference had been made between unearned and earned income. He said that under the income tax duties, the man whose income did not exceed £5OO would receive a rebate of £lO per child. Then there was the super tax upon the man with over £5,000 a year. When he (the speaker) got to £5,000 a year he would pay up and smile, and so would they. hose who earned their money they would only be taxed 9d.in the pound, and to those who did not would have to pay 18. 2d. Referring to the rebate of £lO per child, he said that it was one of the most astute things in the Budget. The workingman who brought up and reared a child was entitled to some recognition, and entitled to some claim.

The death duties would bring in an increase of £3,000,000. He thought that Vk hen a man was cold and in his coffin it was about the best time to pick his pockets. (Laughter and applause.) If those who mime into the dead men's fortunes objected to receive them on the conditions of the increase in the duties, he thought he could find plenty men in Warrington who would be willing to receive thew.( Laughter and applause.) If they would not take them he would,and be would stand it without either wincing or mincing. The Government proposed to raise from to of a million by stamp duty. The Stock and Share Market was not grumbling. They were accepting it as a reasonable increase in con- nection with their business. They also proposed to receive £600,000 by a tax on motor cars, then there was another item, a tax on land values. (Loud applause.) Why should there he such a terrible outcry with regard to the taxation of land values? During the last Tory administrations resolutions were passed in the House of Commons in the first instance by a majority of 70 and in the second by a majority of 00,in favour of the taxation of land values. What on earth were the Tory party going about the country and talking against the taxation they Lad approved? When they came talking about it, it was as well to remind them of the fact. The mistake was that land values were not taxed 25 years ago. There had been an agitation recognising land as peculiar for taxation because there was only a limited amount of it. Nobody could make land. If there were one article that should be taxed it should be land. Those who were the holders of it could sleep at nights and still it went on improving in valueit was an article of which they had a right to say that the increased value should to some extent be appropriated by the whole people and reserve to the owners the capital right. He thought the Budget was, if anything, too modest. (Hear, hear.) Instead of going back to the original value they said they would take it at its value to-day. There was a time when under the feudal system in this country the men who held the land had to contribute something to the State in the shape of soldiers, armed, fed, and clothed. The landlords still retained their lands, but they had edged that off on to other Shoulders. It. was for workingmen to say they would not be juggled any longer. In Cardiff there was a wonderful instance of how the landlord had escaped his responsibility. He referred to the Marquis of Bute. His castle stood on IJ, acres of land. Altogether that meant over half-a-million square yards of land. That was rated at £921. In the same town there was a tailor's shop which steed on 500 yards of land, and that was rented at £917. (Shame!) 1 bat was only a sample of the iniquitous way things were going on in this country. Land in the hands of a few men bad been locked up from public use. That was the reason why the Allotments Act was a dead letter. The speaker gave an instance of how in Newcastle a man who had some land was only contributing on the basis of about 30s. an acre. Under the• Tory Government he was relieved of payment of half the rates on account of the Agricultural Ratings Bill brought in by Mr. Balfour, and we had to 'pay the balance for them. When the town wanted to buy some land for a school he charged £9OO per acre. (Shame !) They were making a begin- ning in the Budget to deal with that great question. (Applause.) He said that in 25 years time many statues would have be erected to Mr. Lloyd-George for having the courage to lay hold of the land monopoly and at last begun to make them contribute something to the maintenance of the State. Concluding, he said, the money which was to be raised by the Budget was going to be utilised for old-age pensions, dreadnoughts, social reform and labour exchanges. (Applause.) Thera was only one question asked which was : Is it possible for the Budget to be tampered with since the Appropriation Bill was passed ?" Mr. KENDALL : No. Ido not think it is possible for the Budget to be tampered with. The only thing is,that it can be absolutely rejected. The only thing they can do is to wince when they pass it.. (Laughter). Mr. WYNNE JONES proposed a vote of thanks to the speaker stir] to the chairman.

a Mr. HOWES, jun., in seconding announced that next week Mr. %V. E. Harvey, M.P., of Chesterfield, would be coming down, and the following week he was trying to get Mt. Robert Lewis of Manchester. (Applause). At the latter meeting be hoped that Mr. Chrimes would be present, when he could put any questions to Mr. Lewis as he thought fit. He also reminded the audience of the Lord Advocate's visit on September 13th. The motion was carrie I unanimously.

div.head: DEATH OF MRS J. S FRANCOMB, A Painful Case of Ptomaine Poisoning.
div.p: DEATH OF MRS J. S FRANCOMB, A Painful Case of Ptomaine Poisoning.
THE INQUEST.

On Wednesday morning the Manchester City Coroner, 11r. E. A. Gibson, held an inquest touching the death of Dorothea Carrie May Francomb, aged 29, wife of Mr. Stanley Francomb, solicitor, practising in Kennedy- street, City, and living at Kelvin Side, Fog-lane, Didsbnry. Mr. Francomb is the eldest son or the late Alderman Francomb, of 'Warrington. When the Coroner entered the Court he expressed regret that he had kept the jury waiting. Mr. Francomb, he mid, was summoned to be present at eleven o'clock. but—it was a gross piece of impertinence—he stayed away and had to be sent for.

Francomb arrived shortly after the Coroner bad taken his seat. He was in great distress. In reply to the Coroner, be stated that his wife was apparently in perfect health up to Sunday, the 15th instant. On that day. Which was very hot, she had two or three slices of beef and some stewed fruit for lunch. He bad a little of the meat. _

. - Later in the day his wife complained of indigestion, and in the evening Dr. Goodfellow was called in. Mrs. Francomb began to vomit and also suffered from diarrhcea. On the following Wednesday she was prematurely confined, and on Sunday she died. No one else in the house had been ill.

On the Thursday, being delighted at the birth of a daughter, he told the two servants that they might go out for an hour. They were away for longer than that time, and when they returned he was angry with them, telling them that was a nice way of returning a kind- ness. One of them said she was leaving on the follow- ing day, and he told her she would have to leave that night. _
The Coroner: Did you lose your temper with them? Mr. Francomb admitted that he did.

Well, you have detained us half an hour to-day. What shall we do with you ?—I have lost my wife, and it has nearly been the death of me. That is not the point. You sent your clerk up to see what time you would be wanted because you had not much time. We should like to know what you have to say?

Francomb said be bad hardly known what be was doing. He was now in the bands of a nurse and a relative. If he bad kept them waiting he apologised most humbly and would gladly pay .£5 rather than offend the court.
The Coroner said the explanation would be accepted. The two servants said they had the same food as Mr. Francomb and his wife on the 15th inst. without experi- encing any ill-effects.

Dr. GoOdfellow said be was perfectly satisfied that Mrs. Francomb's death was due to ptomaine poisoning. That opinion was confirmed by another doctor, who also visited Mrs. Francomb. It was quite possible that of several persons partaking of the same food only one might suffer from ptomaine poisoning. The jury returned a verdict of death from misadven- ture through ptomaine poisoning.

BY ANNIE 0. TIBBITS.
Author of "The Love that Won," "Hunted Down," "Hidden Hands," "The Finger of Fate." "Robes of Shame." ex. CHAPTER XV.

As Olga slipped out of the room Edward closed the door, and stood for a moment look- ing straight in front of him. Geoffrey lifted his head and nodded to him, but he did not see. He was looking at Julia. He went towards her, and Ethel, who liaci paused in her playing, looked up just in time to see him give a quiet, almost , impercept- ible nod to Julia. Ethel looked 'quickly to- wards her, and the extraordinary pallor of her face startled her a little.
But it was only for a moment. The next Edward had taken his scat and Ethel had turned to Dick again. She looked up into his face while her hands wandered -lightly upon the keys.
"Have you done anything yet?" she wills. pered. "Have you beeh making inquiries? " He nodded.

"I am looking up the papers and the ac- counts of the trial," he whispered back. "There are heaps of them to go through, but I shall work hard—and hope." "Yes—and hope." She smiled into his face Her music drifted suddenly into a waltz, and the light brightened in her eyes. "Oh, I be- lieve you will succeed," she whispered. "I believe everything will be all right. I almost feel as if things were all right." "Don't—don't," he cried. "Sometimes when one feels sure of a thing something turns up and upsets it. Don't feel sure yet. It almost seems too good to hope for, and may fail." Her eyes sobered. The waltz grew slower under her touch.
"You won't fail—you won't fail," she said under her breath. He bent down.
"I have so much at stake," he said. "Ti makes me afraid, but sometimes I think I cannot lose my happiness a second time." "No, no--you won't. You will succeed," she cried.
She stopped playing, and at that instant Julia stirred in her seat and bent towards Geoffrey. _

"Sir Geoffrey," she cried, "Mr. Verriker says you have got a Bluebeard's room in the house. Have you?" Geoffrey looked up. "I, Miss Dunston? " he cried, -in mock horror. "I assure you I am not guilty. I have not even got a ivife as yet. And that reminds me, Ethel, why did Olga go away?" Ethel looted round quickly. She did not even know she had gone. Meanwhile Edward was explaining to Geoffrey. "Perhaps you have not discovered it yet," he said. "But there is a real Bluebeard'b chamber in the Hall. Very few people know about it, and as it is supposed to be haunted it is always kept a secret from the servants:"
"A hatinted room!" cried Ethel. "Oh, how exciting! Why, nobody has ever whis- pered a word about a ghost to us. Are you sure, Edward?"

Edward was standing up, tugging ner- vously at his moustache. The deep, straight Lines from nose to mouth were more pro- nounced than ever. His eyes had a bright, feverish look as he glanced, first at one face and then at another, and finally at the carpet underfoot.

"Yes, I am perfectly sure," he answered; "in fact, I could shew you the room. It is always kept locked, and the key that fits it is the key of uncle's room—your room now, Geoffrey. It is the only key in the house that will open it." Ethel came forward from the piano. "But what is the secret of the room?" she asked. "Why is it haunted? Is there any story about it? Oh, do tell us," Edward shook his head.

"I don't know," he said, slowly. "I never heard the real truth about it. As I say, no one ever mentioned the room, but I think I remember hearing that a child died there once, and that it cries, or something of that sort. But I never heard of anyone hear- ing it." Nor I," said Mrs. Verriker. "We have not heard it, at any, rate, and had no idea that there was such a thing as a haunted room, even though the place is old enough to have one." "Every old house ought to have a ghost," said Ethel. "Well, I'm glad we are fashion- able. But, Edward, which room is it? I shan't rest in my bed to-night if I don't knue." Edward turned with his eyes on Julia, and she looked. up with a queer light in hers. _ . _ _

"Couldn't we see it 1" she -cried. "I have never been in a haunted room. Sir Geoffrey, do let us go and see it. May we?" She paused, and for a moment anyone who had been watching her would have seen her hold her breath.
"Well, I don't mind," said Geoffrey, "if Edward will lead the way and shew us where it is."

Edward shrugged his shoulders. " I wish I hadn't mentioned it," he said. "There is something uncanny about this room. They say some queer accidents have happened there.' Ethel clapped her hands suddenly. "I know where it is," she cried. "How silly of us. It is that door next to Geoffrey's room which nobody could open, and the ser- vants said it had been fastened up from in- side. Oh, of course, I remember. They said .there was a secret way to it, only nobody knew it, and nobody had been able to dis- cover it, and Sir Henry wouldn't let anybody explore. Don't you remember, mother. Bates told us that the first week we came, and we have never bothered about it since. But do let's go and see. Edward, do you think there are any Bluebeard's wives there hanging in a row? Do you think we shall see anything horrible? Well, I am ready. I shan't mind anything—even a skeleton—" "Don't let her go, Geoffrey," said Edward, suddenly. " I wish I hadn't mentioned it. There are strange stories about that room." "Oh, don't listen to him, Geoffrey," Ethel cried. "What can happen? Do come along." Edward stepped forward. His yellow fore- head was glistening now, his face was work- ing oddly. You go first," he said, in a strange, husky voice. "I shan't go near the place. I don't believe in exploring things of that kind, but if you go, Geoffrey, you go first." "Oh, I'll go first," cried Geoffrey. "You need not fear; and, anyhow, I feel a bit curious about it. Yes, we'll go. Who is atoming? " Mrs. Verriker hesitated with a vague, nervous look on her face. She looked at Edward, and Isis air -of excitement alarmed her a little. But, then, Edward always had been a weak, excitable, foolish creature, and he looked a coward now,, and, after all, what could possibly happen,? She turned slowly. s. Dunston and Julia had sprung up. Old Pendlebury stood quietly for a moment, and then he inter- rupted. I fancy I remember something," he said, "but I don't think the room was haunted. There was something else. If I could only remember—"
Julia sent a quick, anxious glance at him and then at Edward.

"Oh, come, do let us go," she said, im- patiently. "Don't try to remember, Mr. Pendlebury. We will go and find out." Geoffrey led the way into the hall. "There ts plenty of light in the corridor, but we had better take candles as well," he said. " We will light them upstairs." He handed one to everybody, and then the:; were ready; Ethel excited and voluble, and Julia quiet and expectant, breathing a little skarply as they began to ascend the great sraircase. The men were silent. Only Mr. Perullebury went on with his reminiscences. "1 remember Sir Henry speaking of it once," he said. "I believe he wanted to have it opened, -if I remember rightly. But I can't recollect what he said was the mystery connected with it. It wasn't exactly a mys- tery, but a secret hiding-place, or something Pe that, but I am not sure if be mentioned

what it was exactly. However, we shall see directly." They had reached the head of the stair- case and faced the corridor. Geoffrey and Ethel were first, and Mrs. Vcrriker followed close upon their heels. Edward hung back a little, but as they walked down the corridor his, voice, harsh and husky, followed them. . . . _

" Don't let her go in," he 'cried. "No one knows what accident may happen." "All right," Geoffrey called back, and then suddenly, sharply, he stood still. "What was that?" ho cried. "Did you hear anything, Ethel? " They all stopped, standing in a little huddled crowd, motionless in the great cor- ridor.
It was someone crying," Geoffrey said in a low voice, and Mrs. Verriker gave a quick shudder.

"The child," she whispered, "the ghost !" "Nonsense," said Geoffrey, a little sharply, and went on again. As he went he stared ahead along the corridor. "Ethel, where is Olga?" he asked, sud- denly, without turning his head. ," What be- came of her? Hark ! " He stood still again. "It Is someone calling," he, said. Again they all huddled close together, a queer company in evening dress, with their faces growing slowly white, with two faces behind, eager, nervous, waiting with fiendish anxiety for the " accident " to happen. These two faces hung back in the shadow, silent and terrible, as Geoffrey again moved slowly forward. He had reached the door of his room now, and he stopped to take out the key. At the same moment the cry came again—a low, faint, broken cry. _ _

- "Good heavens !" cried the doctor. "That's no ghost, but a human being in pain." Geoffrey hurried forward, and with a stride reached the door of the Bluebeard's room. There he stopped, checked by Ethel, who had caught his arm.
"Don't go-in," she cried. "I am afraid." "hark !
They stood in silence, and then the groan- ing cry came again. It's from the room itself, and, good heavens the door_ is open ! " cried Geoffrey.

"Don't go in!" Cried Ethel, suddenly. "Oh, Geoffrey, don't go without a light." She struck a match and lighted one of the candles. Her hands were trembling strangely. Some fear which she could not comprehend had seized her.
It is said that sometimes persons aro affected by the presence of evil people. Per- haps she was affected by the presence of those two evil faces behind her, the two faces that watched and waited.

Anyhow, she handed Geoffrey flu') candle with a feeling of fear and horror that WAS strange 41. her, for generally she knew no fear. But her face was white, and ,her eyts wild as she followed Geoffrey to the owl door. Dick was beside her. He put his ha& d on her shoulder, and then they all came to a standstill behind Geoffrey, peering over his shoulder at the empty r00m....
Geoffrey held no the-candle. Then he went

draggel tier to Inin in the darkness, and with his hexrt suddenly standing still he felt the nail came out with his efforts, and fall clanking and ringing against the sides of the well. Only a miracle had saved her life to-night!
_ Ho folded her close, and began slowly mounting the ladder again. She lay heavy in his arms, and, as he went, something warm and sticky 'trickled over his face.
At the 'top he handed her carefully into the arms stretched out for her, and then put his hand to his face and, drawing it away, looked at it. It was covered with blood!
A minute later he had crawled out, and war half sitting, half lying, sick and faint, beside Olga on the floor.
The doctor bent over her with a grey and anxious face.
"Is she all right—is she all right?" Geof- frey cried. But the doctor gave no answer.
CIIAPTER XVI.

Julia and Edward stood in the corridor staring at each other with white faces. Ed- ward shrank back in the shadow, coward written upon his whole, crouching figure. "You must have left the door wide open," Julia whispered harshly. "Oh, what a fool you have been!" •" I shut it," Edward replied, obstinately. "I remember drawincv it to after me—l thought I locked "Thought!" cried Julia, contemptuously. " I know I shut it," Edward said; and Julia turned on him, her face blazing in the di.ai light of the corridor. "Then how did she know about it?" she whispered. "If you didn't leave tho door wide open, as I say you did, how did she get to know of the room? Don't be a fool, Edward. You have failed just through one small thing—failed! Oh, if you had only locked the door!"

"Yes, I have failed," he whispered, bit- terly. "I shall always fail." Julia's face grew c'ark. "We shall not fail again," she said. "We have failed now, but we shall not fail again." The two stood' apart from the group about Olga's silent figure on the floor. They were at so busy over ber that no one noticed them. and in the shadow Julia suddenly turned and slipping her arm into Edward's bent her face close to his.

"We shall not fail next time," she wbis pored, harshly; "but now, for heaven's sake, go, and don't let them see that there is any- thing amiss. Go forward as if you knew no- thing. You must pretend that it was the stories about the room that unnerved you. Do you hear? Edward, speak. Do you hear? Go. Don't 4S •NAL fool—go. Do you care about me? Do you ant me? Then go ! " He went quickly as if he had suddenly realised that he was on the verge of losing her. Her words galvanised him into life, and grey of face, with his shifty eyes and his hair (-amp about his yellow forehead, he went into the Bluebeard's chamber. "I knew something would happen." he

div.p: ' He folded her close, and began s

step nearer. The light threw strange flickering shadows about it, shewing it large and almost empty. It looked almost like an attic into which lumber had been throwri, for in the flickering, unsteady light the one or two chairs looked old and worm-eaten, and a great chest that was thick with (lust looked as if it had been there for hundreds of years. Geoffrey lowered the candle and threw the light on the floor, and then the yawning hole caught his eye. He fell back. As he did .t) the cry came again, so close, so clear, that the perspira- tion broke out upon his forehead, and, tak- ing a step forward, he flung himself upon his knees before the hole.
"Good heavens, it's Olga!" he cried. He peered down. Darkness spread before him—deep and utter darkness. He took the candle, and, shading it, tried to throw the light into the shaft. _ _

It's Olga!" he cried, wildly. "Olga— Olga darling—can you hear? Can you hear?" He waited for the answer, and ' faintly, feebly the answer came. "What on earth does it mean?" he cried. "How on earth did she come here? And this hole. . . . It's incomprehensible. But how are we to get at her?" He peered down, and then suddenly something caught his eye. "There is a ladder here," he cried. "Doctor, you hold the light while I go down."
Mrs. Verriker sprang forward. "No—no,- Geoffrey, don't run any risk," he cried. "The ladder may be rotten—you may fall."

'`Mother, She is down there," he cried. "I must go." She fell away again, and he turned, hold- ing on to the floor, and feeling with his foot, until at last he placed it firmly on the first rung of the ladder. It was iron, and he gave a little sigh of relief. It was sound enough. He took another step downward. Olga's voice had faded again and grown into a vague, unconscious moan. Geoffrey looked up as he went down and saw above him a ring of white faces. Ho saw the doctor hold the candle to Dick and turn to follow, but he stopped him. "Don't come," he cried. "I wilf call if I want you. I shall be all right." He descended into the darkness. It seemed a long way, and the flickering candle - light seemed like the light of a match, when at bust lie heard the low moaning voice close to his. ear. He stretched out his hand.

" Olga darling," ho cried. On every side his fingers came in contact with stonework, like the walls of a well. It was deep, and icy cold, and a draught seined to rush up from an open sp!iee_ at the bottom.

"Olga darling," he whispered, but there was no answer; and, taking another step downwards, he put out his hand again. This time it came in contact with some- thing different from the stonework—something soft and flimsy. Gingerly he felt, and care- fully ho stretched out his arms until he felt her slight body, and then—then he gave a sob of relief. "Thank heaven! Oh, thank heaven!" The strangest and slightest accident had saved her. A hook in the wall had caught in her frock as she fell. He urew cold all over as
