sAict naraniy, as the ooctor still bent over Olga. "Uncle didn't have the room locked up for nothing, and I warned you before we came-
yes," said Mrs. Verriker; "but listen."

The doctor had turned and was speaking to her. "Wo will get her to bed now, please," he said; and as he rose to help carry her,. Geoffrey caught his arm again. "Is she all right? Will she be all right?" he cried.
"I can't tell you yet," said tho doctor. "We must wait."

Hours afterwards he was still waiting while Olga struggled slowly through the night. She seemed to be in a nightmare, and, suddenly, as the dawn was breaking, she started up, turning to Ethel and catching her Ann. "He won't forget that I saved his life," she cried, in a sobbing whisper. "Oh ! thank heaven I saved his life, and whatever cornea —whatever he hears of me—he won't forget that—that I loved him enough for that." She sank back again and the .doctor rose. "We shall see now," he said; "it may be brain fever or it may be nothing. In an hour we shall see."
He looked at her a little doubtfully. Her white face against the white sheets looked woefully thin and worn and fragile. She Looked just then as if a wind would blow her away._ _

"-She has just -come through a bad expeii- ance, too," he said, thoughtfully. I'm afraid of "shock. The wreak at sea and now this are enough to upset anyone. If she says wild things don't be surprised. If she imagines things and talks of things which have never happened, you will understand it is what I expect. lam afraid of brain fever, but—but perhaps she will pull through. She is not seriously hurt. That knock on the head is bad, but not serious. It is only the shock to the nerves that I am• really afraid of. But, 'anyhow, in the morning we shall see."

In the morning he was agreeably surprised. Olga lay still, open-eyed, and calm, and rational. The only thing the matter was her head, and that ached and throbbed and jumped until she could scarcely see him as he bent over her. It prevented her thinking, too, and she looked up at lint a little wildly. "What day is it?" she asked. "Friday," he answered. "Do you re- member last night? " She nodded, and he saw a quick shiver pass over her.

"Well; you remember you fell down a shaft in one of the rooms, and Sir Geoffrey crawled dowd after you and .brought you up; and now he is very anxious about you. Would you like to see him? She. nixlcled. Yes, for the last time—for the very last time. Directly she got rid ,of this headache, directly she could raise Ivor head from the pillow, she would write her letter and leave him. But, meanwhile, she would see him now, for the last time. • She had forgotten Dr. Dacre, and that ho might be at the Hall to-day. She rememberc‘i only last night, and how close Geoffrey had been to death, and that she had done him her last service—she had risked her life for his.

She lay very still while she waited for him to come. Ethel came and bent over her, her bright face looking anxiously into hers. • Well, old dear?" she said. Olga suddenly put up her arms. "Ethel, you have been good to me," she said, brokenly, "you and your mother and Geof- frey have been too goad. But it could not Last, and I—l am thankful even to have had these few days—before the end." _ _
Ethel lookeel clown in alarm. "What nonsense are you talking?" she cried.

Olga's arms clung ahouit her. " You will think the best—Ethel, will you promise that, whatever comes, you Will re- member me only as you have known me these r.ew days? Will you promise? You have liked me, haven't you? Oh, promise to re- member only that —only that you have liked me,' and that—that I was thank ful --oh, yes, thankful for all your goodness to me. I scarcely dare think of ir, Ethel dear, but it has all been so good that even the worst—will be easier now."

Ethel stooped and kissed her, and put her hand tend'erly on the bandage about her head. They had evidently thought her out of the wood too soon. She was beginning to talk wildly, as the doctor had thought she would.

"Yes, dear," she said', gently, "of course we shall. Only you munn't bother now. Lie still, and I will send Geoffrey to you." She ran out of the room, and met him in the corridor. She caught his arm. "Geoffrey, be very careful with her," she cried. " She is saying all sorts of wild things. The doctor said she wou!d, mei I. am going to tell him she is doing so before be leaves the house. She has got the funniest ideas in her head. She seems to think that she is going. I am afraid she has got the idea in her head that she is very ill, or something, and that she may die, for she is talking of it. Go and stop her, Geoffrey dear, while I run after the doctor."

She flew along the corridor and downstairs to the hall doer. No brongham stood outside, and she turned breathlessly to the butler, who was crossing the hall. "How long' has the doctor. becn gone?" she asked.

" Only this very instant, miss," was the reply. s" Then go after him, and try to bring him baCk," Ethel cried ; and, as the butler ran out, she followed him down the leng drive and part way_ across the park. The doctor's carriage was in sight, and a shout brought him back. She gave her message to him. 6` I don't think there is any danger *mow," he said; "but I'll go back and have another look at her, just to satisfy you." "But she is talking nonsense, t;•octor, as you said she would; and I believe she thinks she is going to die." The doctor smiled a BUIE, but he went back. Ethel remained for a moment. Some- one was coming along the drive, and she stood shading her eyes in the sun to see who it was.
"Who is it, Bates ?", she said to the butler. "Do you recognise him ? " Bates screened his eyes, and waited moment before he replied. Then he shook his head.
"It's no one that I have ever seen before,' he said.
"Well, we won't wait for him. We'll follow the doctor."'

She turne6 as she spoke, and walked slowly back towards the house. It was a lovely morning, threatening another hot day. The sun streamed over the park from a cloudless blue sky. Everything • was silent and breath- less and hot.

It was just such another day as the day on which the Stella haa gene down in mid- ocean. Just such another day as that on which the sea had been blue and smooth and still, and death had stared the passengers of the Stella in the face. Not a breath of wine stirred the leaves of the trees in the park. Not a cloud shewed upon the sky, and under- foot- the last drop of dew had gone from the hot earth.
Ethel drew a deep breath as she reached the great porch, an dropped for a moment on the stonework to get cool before she went indoors.

The man came on slowly up the drive. Ethel watched him curiously. ' seemed al- most reluctant to come, and with a vague in- terest she kepc her face turned to him. - As he came nearer, she saw that he leoked a gentleman, and also that he looked ill. He was tall and thin, dresse in a navy-blue suit and a straw hat, and he • seemed to bear rather heavily -upon the stick he carried. When she saw that she got up sharply and walked to meet him. ,He was certainly ill, auu he was not exactly a young man. She quickened her steps a little, and then she iaw clearly that his face was drawn, and grey, and thin, and that there was grey in , hiF hair and grey in the weak moustache that covered his lips. He raised his hat as he saw her, and she stopped before- him. There was something curious about him. In spite of his evide& ill-health he looked determined and stern, and seemed strung up to a pitch of endur- ance. Perhaps he was suffering. He stopped, hat in hand, and looked steadily into her girlish face. _ _ _ _
"Is this Kemseiite Hu?" he asked.
Ethel nodded, and he hesitated as though it was difficult for him to speak. Ho looked out across the park and then back at Ethel's fa cl before he did so.
I wanted," he said, slowly, "to ask if there is a Miss Murray staying hero?" Ethel's eyes brightened, and he wondered a little as he. saw her smile.

"Why, yes, of course she is," she cried. "Did you wish to see her? She—she is - not very well this morning. There was an acci- dent last night and she was hurt. I am rather afraid that she may be seriously hurt." "Seriously hurt." He repeated the words dully, staring at her as though he did not see her, as though his thoughts were far away. "I am afraid so, though the doctor didn't think so an hour ago , when he saw her;• but he has gone back now, and then we shall see."

The man leant on his stick. His face was the strangest Ethel thought she had ever seen—the face of a young man grown old, the face of a young man aged before his time. Then I shall not be able to see her " Ile asked.

"I am afraid not. You see, she is in bed. and the doctor says she is to lie there all day, for she got a nasty knock on her head, and it may be very bad. Poor Olga! She had a narrow escape of her life last night!" The man started, and Ethel looked up._
"Are you a friend of hers?" she asked, eagerly. "Did you want to see her very badly?" He hesitated, and again his eyes wandered slowly over the park and then back to Ethel's face.

"Has she ever spoken- to you of a Dr. Dacre? " he asked, suddenly. Ethel thought for a moment, and then her face brightened and a little mischievous sparkle flashed in her eyes as she remem- bered Geoffrey's remarks of last night. "Oh, are you the Dr. Dacre who was on board the ship?." she cried. " Oh, of course she has. Why, Geoffrey was only speaking of you last night. You will come and see him, won't you?" Again Dr. Dacre hesitated. His lips twitched under his thin moustache and his hands clenched over his stick. _ _

• " Perhaps—l think perhaps I ,will," he , said, slowly. 'Ethel turned. "You look as if you had been ill," she said after a moment, "and we saw in the papers that you had been picked -droadfully exhausted. Geoffrey and Olga were luckier. I am sure they will both be delighted to see you." , He winced a little and looked at her sharply. "I wrote to Miss Murray yester- day," he said. " Did she have my letter, do you know?" • -Ethel shook her head. " She did not say," she replied, "but I remember there was a letter for her- last night. I expect the acci- dent drove it out of her mind." They stood in silence for a minute or two. Dr. Dacre scarcely turned his .head. His eyes were fixed on the house.
"Is—i 4 your brother very fond of Miss Murray?" he asked, abruptly, and Ethel turned quickly, laughing a little at the ques- tion.
" Fond? " she began. "Why, I never srr,v anybody so desperately in love; I never saw

two people so absorbed in each other. 'they are lovely---" She stopped, checked by a look on his face, and by the memory of .Geoffrey's words of last night. She remembered that Dr. Dacre had, been in love With Olga too. That was the reason why he had come, of course— to see Olga, perhaps in the hope that she would become his wife. She looked at his face with a new interest and sighed. He must be very fond of her to comm after her so soon. He must have come straight from the sea to her. Poor man! He had stopped in the middle of the path. "I think as Miss Murray is not well I . will not come in," he said, slowly. "I will wait." "But we are so close to the house," Ethel urged, "and it is so hot. Do come in and get cool before you walk back." He shook his head. His face had growr very grey and set. ".No, I will come again,' he., said. Perhaps...to:morrow. I .can wait.' •
"But Geoffrey will be cross with me fot letting. you go."

" hini I will come again. Or wait, no don't tell him you have seen me. Don't sax anything to him, but to Miss Murray—tefi Miss Murray that I will see her to-morroo if she is well enough." Ethel stared at him. It seemed curious, and she hesitated.
"Of course, you know that Miss Murray going to marry my brother?" she said.

He- nodded -stifffy. "I guessed," he said "Yes, I guessed." Something terribly old and worn on hi! face went suddenly to Ethel's heart. Sh 4 held out her hand impulsively. "And you will come to-morrow?" sh 4 said. "But; what is your address? Woule you like Geoffrey to come and see you? 1 suppose you will be staying in Kennet ? " X° nodded his head. "For long?" Ethel asked. He turned away. "Until my purpose ij accomplished," he said. • Then he left her abruptly, and Ethel stood watching his feeble, bent, unsteady figurt until it was out of sight. . "What a funny man," she said. "What on earth could he have meant by that?"
(To be Continued.)

div.p: WOMEN'S GHAT.

Mr. and Mrs. Asquith in Kent. —Lympne Castle, where Mrs. Asquith and her children have been staying, is situated in that quiet old-world corner of Kent near the, Like many distinguished people, the Prime Minister and Mrs. Asquith have been prevented from going to Scotland by the prolonged Parliamentary session, and midst needs be content with brief holidays taken within easy distance of London. Elizabeth Carter, the poetess lived at Lympne Hill, and records how that pArt of Kent was disturbed in her time by fears of a French invasion. In December' 1745, the French were . hourly expected to make a descent on Dungeness, ar, owing to contrary winds, the English fleet could not move from the Doena, whilst the weather was favourable for the French. "If they landed" wrote Miss Carter, "they must come to London by Lympne Hill, end the defenceless." The Nlnrtello Towers, now' obsolete as a means of defence, lut still a familiar object en the coast from Beachy head to Hythe, sere not built until the latter part of the eighteenth century, when the country was once more alarmed by the prospect of a French invasion tinder Napoleon. The New Red Cross Scheme.—Tbere is a place for 'everyone in our new Territoi ial army for home defence. The boy joins the Scouts, and his little sister is already clamouring for a similar organisation of scoutesses. Then doctors, chemists and trained nurses have been enlisted on the staffs of the general base hospitals, which would be fully Equipped in the event of war, and there are to be the local Red Cross detachments, organ- ised on the voluntary principle in the towns and villages throughout the country, so as to be able to render skilled first-aid to the pounded. There is an did- standing and widespread belief that nursing can be undertaken by anyone' but in reality it is an art which can only Le acquired by training. The Red Cress scheme would bring the services of trained and helpful people within its organisation and we may be sure it will not appeal in vain to the village doctor, and the village nurse, as well as others who could help in making the medical and hospital service thoroughly efficient in a time of national emergency.

Railway Travelling.—llining cars are now a feature of all long railway journeys, and make it easy for us to visit distant holiday resorts to which our parents con- sidered the journey too long and tedious. The Great Northern Railway, running from London, which is con- templating the abolition of first and second class carri- ages, and adopting third class for all, was the first Company to introduce the dining car into this country. That was in 1879, shortly after the Midland liailway had imported " Pullman car a from America. The oft- predicted abolition of first and second class carriages would, if it comes about, affect women more than men. The latter will go third class when alone, but first and second when travelling with their wives and families, and many women prefer to pay for the greater privacy and comfort of the better classes. It will probably be many years before any great change is made, although the fact that so many rich people use motor-cars instead of the railways for their travelling will not be without its influence in bringing this about. The Two Shilling Novel.—Coinciding with the flood of autumn fiction, Mr. Heinemann -begins the experi- ment of publishing novels at 2s. and 3s. each, according to length, If a book is too large for one volume, it is run into two, as in the case of Mr. Hall Caine's new novel "The V% hite Prophet" which is issued by Mr. Heioemaon in ON° volumes at 2s. each. It, is a story of Egypt and of the British occupation. There is nothing in which the public suffer so much from "short weight " as in the baying of books, and we should welcome Mr. Heinemasn's endeavour to deal fairly and squarely with the reading public. It should also tend to improve the quality of fiction. Many a story is worsened and lengthened out by the process of padding "in order to decently fill a 6s. volume. In its natural length, it it weuld be ample fox a 2s: book, and that would not only give the public the story at its best but also value for money. -

Summer Hoesekeeping.—The vagaries of our climate make it difficult for us to regulate our dress and house- hold arrangements according to the almanac. If we get a really hot spell, we "muddle through" it, according to cur national custom of meeting other difficulties, but it would help a great deal if housekeeping were more adapted to climate conditions, and not so much run on lines of a fixed routine, summer and winter alike. To break avkayfrom these traditions would seem heretical. iAt least it s so in the great majority of households, whereas work inigliehe eased in hot weather by reduced cooking, an earlier breakfast, and only doing necessary household labour. It. is a great misfortune for a woman to feel herself held a slave to the house, and a little ingenuity would often go far in reducing the work of running it. Concerning Stings.—Dolightful as meals out of doors prove in beautiful weather there are certain drawbacks to take into consideration, such as insects dropping off the trees into our plates, or drinking receptacles, the attraction good things of the table have for wasps, and the chance that the bees may mis- take our delicacies for their legitimate quarry on garden bushes and walls. Provided the bees and wasps wonld leave us alone however, we could manage to put up with their raids' but unfortunately they occasionally do nothing of the kind, and their stings this year are proving exceptionally severe. Many remedies are offered us, and some undoubtedly prove highly efficacious, but it must be remembered that a very great teal indeed depends upon the promptness with which they are applied. The blue bag, damped and placed over the wound is a very old-fashioned notion, so also is the application of olive oil, honey. pure lemon juice, or a paste of flour and water, while other authorities insist upon the value of drops of hartshorn applied immediately. Faithful to Foulard.—Contrary to expectation, foulard is still worn by smart dressers,a state of affairs probably due in great measure to the weather, which this season has sadly interfered with the donning of airy-fairy clothes. Foulard seems to fill .a gap between the warm and airy-fairy, and it possesses moreover the further advantage of lending itself to the simplest possible style, or much elaboration. It has been said, and truly, that a foulard gem n can be worn in the morning, and worn equally well in the afternoon—differently cut and built of course. Spots are considered the best design, and these for the most part are large, and in the same hue as the background, only lighter or darker, as choice dictates.

Tailor-land.—Tailors are greatly disposed to finish off coats of linen, cotton, or other fabric destined for the " tub " with satin collars, which means that only the dry cleaner can wrestle with these garments when they become soiled. There is something very smart-looking about the alliance, at the same time it is not a possible one for those whose purses are light. Another departure in tailor-land lies in the fastening of coats beneath the aaist only; instead of across the bust, and yet another, allowing greater length at the back than in front. For some time past coats have been longer in front than behind, a notion of which we have apparently grown tired.

_ The Hatless Brigade.—The hatless ones have now taken to tying up their heads in motor veils, a procedure that certainly can not be considered desirable from any point of view. It emphatically does not make for smartness, and moreover entirely fails to provide the shade so necessary for the wellbeing of the complexion. There is nothing more conducive to a crop of wrinkles about tbo eyes and mouth, than a spell of "going hat- less " as many girls and women have found to their cost. MADGE.

The /jury returned a verdict of "Found drowned," and wired the ccroner to censure the parents, ar.d this Coroner Brighouse did very severely. NEWTON FLOWER SHOW. The 24th annual show of the Newton-le-Willows Horticultural Society was held in the field behind Mr. Randall's Nurseries on Saturday. Though rain fell heavily during the morning the afternoon was much more favourable, and as a result the attendance, whilst not a record, was a very satisfactory one The entries numbered nearly 600, and the exhibits generally were of a very high-class character, competition in all the classes being exceptionally keen. The two prize-winners in the class for groups of miscellaneous plants arranged for effect, NI ere magnificent specimens of the art of horticulture. In the cut flowers section there were some splendid speoiewns of dahlias and gladioli, whilst among the fruit, the grapes and apples were very high class.— During the afternoon a capital sports programme of 13 events was gone through, and some good racing was seen. At intervals displays with clubs and bar-bells and in free movements and pyramids were given by six members of the Vulcan Physical Drill Class, under the direction of Mr. R. J. Hill (instructor). At the close the prizes were presented to the sports winners by Mrs. L. h. Whittaker. During the afternoon selections were played on the field by the Earlestown Prize Band, who also played for dancing in the evening.

Lymm. NEW CHAPEL AT BROOMEDGE. OPENING CEREMONY. Primitive Methodists at Broomedge, Lymm, es ill henceforth be able to worship on their own premises instead of, as they have been doing for years past, on Anglican, for on Wednesday afternoon a new chapel capable of seating 150 persons, was opened by Miss Eleanor Cross of Broomecige. The chapel which cost £6OO including a freehold site is to be used as a school- room as well. The chapel is of ordinary brick and has a tower at the front. There is a main body, min:sters' vestry, two lavatories, small gallery and vestibule. There are forms to sit on and on the platform rests the pulpit. There is also an American organ which cost .10 guineas. The windows are of the leaded light type, and the lighting is on the incandescent system. The builder was Mr. .1. H. Holt, of Lymm, and Messrs. J. D. and S. J. Mould the architects. The Rev. R. W. B. Whiteway presided over the open- ing ceremony and amongst those present were: Revs. H. Haynes, J. W. Fryer (Chester), Ccuncillor G. L. Welforil, Messrs. .1. H. Holt, J. W. Cross, H. Bencroft (Timperley), William Davies (Bollington), and E. Jones (organist). There was a good attendance despite seceial showers. The Chairmen said it wee thought by a number of friends that what honour there was in connection with the opening of the new chapel it should he placed upon a family that was closely associated with Primitive Methodism at Broom Ede. Miss Cross's mother who died recently, was me st interested in the cause and she had worked for many years in the hope and expectation of seeing a Low chapel in the neighbourhood. He thought that there was no person more eligible than Miss Cross to perform the duty of opening the chapel. He then handed the hey to Miss Cross who, previous to inserting it in the lock and opening the door,said she had great pleasure in opening that door for the glory of God and for the blessing of the people in the neighbour- hood. She hoped it would be a Bethel for their souls. (Applause,) The audience then went into the chapel. The dedicatory service wss then commenced, the sermon being preached by the Rev. J. W. Fryer, in the ccurse of which he said we all wanted pleasure and immediate profit out of religion, and we shrunk from the penalty that attechcd to it. If we could have the pleasure without the pain then we would have an easy mind, but pain accompanied pleaeure. If we were to ask ourselves why itwes that we worshipped, we would say we felt it a duty to our Creator to acknowledge His kindness and His mercy. Others might say that they had a nature that aspired to spiritual, invisible real things and in God's House they transcended their senses. Others said there was nothing ro refreshing to them- selves as the quiet hour of prayer and the detachment from labour. Others said that to them worship we§ the prelude to duty. They learned in the House of God in meditation red prayer what was their duty, and how best they could serve God and their fellow men. Others would say that to them the gn at value of worship was communion with saints. All those answers were perfectly good and perfectly right. It sesmed to him that there was a foundation first beneath them all. That fivandetion was confession of sin end its forgive- ness. That was the foundation of Christianity. Some- thing was involved in the Cress—sufferiag, expiation, sacrifice and atonement. The keynote to Christ's life was.the removing of the burden of sin, and wherever there had been an outburst of religion it had had two causes. It had arisen from a profound sense of human unworthiness, and it had created a form of religious expression to denote the new sense of unworthiness. '1 here bad not been a revival through religion without a teen sense of sin and a quick sense of forgiveness. Con- cluding, the preacher said that it was not the place wherein they worshipped narticularly, but it was the spirit they breathed. Men worshipped God under divetee conditions,but as long as they were devout they always found God In the evening a meeting wrs held in the chapel, Mr. J. H. Holt presiding over a large attendance. The speakers were Principal W. Jones-Davies (Hartley College' Manchester), Revs. J. W. Fryer, R. B. White- way G. Mitchell and Haynes. • LYMM COUNCIL. div.head: POSTAL FACILITIES.
div.p: POSTAL FACILITIES.

The Clerk read a letter rom the Liverpool Post Office asking the Council if they could postpone the hour of opening Lymm Post Office from 7 a.tu to 8 a.m. They also desired the sanction of the Council for Heatley Heath Post Office to be closed on Wednes- days from 1 p.m. to 7 p.m. The alteration would not make any alteration in the despatch of letters or the collection of them. Any telegrams received for licatley Heath would be delivered from Lymm Post Office. Mr. Warburton sAid he did not object to the Sub- postmaster having a half-holiday. He thought it was a right and proper thing, but at the Arne time he thought that some authorised person should be placed in the Pest Office whilst he was away,because it was a quickly growing district and there were some important tele- grams that came to Heatley and district. If they had to send tel. grams back again it meant that they would have to go to Lymm to send them. He did not think they ought to close it having regard to that. . Mr. Gotobed said nothing would prevent them from telephoning the message to Lymm. Mr. Warburton: 1. am afraid there is no one that will take on the responsibility. Mr. Groves: They are asking our opinion, but won't tly)y please themselves? Mr. Ewart : Of course they will. _ _

Mr. Welford moved: "That the Council having no means of rscertaining whether it would be a conveni- ence or inconvenience, that the matter be left with the Post Otnce authorities to decide, they having knowledge of the facts." Mr. Evcart seconded. Mr. Warburton moved as an amendment: "That the public convenience demands that the Post °lke at fieatley be kept open." _
Mr. Mostonsecnded. On the amendment being put to the Council, two voted for it and three against. The resolution V% ELS then put and was c rr:ed by three to two.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH GARDEN SOCIETY.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH GARDEN SOCIETY.
ANNUAL SHOW.

It may be truly said that the e:ghth annual show, fancy dress parade and sports which were held on Saturday in Mr. Henry. Greenall's grounds under the auspices of the Stockton Heath Garden Society were the finest both in point of class and number of entries in the district. Ihe earlier part of the day was characterised by inclement weather, and even at the opening by Lady Greens!!, it was not altogether pleasant, but later it was simply lovely, the sun's rays blending harmoniously with the various eshibita.During the afternoon the Territorial Band,under the conductor- ship of Mr. J. T. Richardson, played several selections, and in the evening the Scciety's orchestra, led by Mr. W. E. Ray, played selections, dancing also being engaged in. The entri‘r, which numbered more than GOO, were , artistically arranged in three large teats and both their quality and the effect of ;he setting out was much to be admired. Looking in one direction one saw several dishes of fruit exhibited by P.Wilkinson and which won a deserved first prize. There were six dishes .cora- posed of golden and Waal( grapes, peaches, melon, pine- apple, and greengages. One turned suddenly round and was confronted as ith quite a contrast in the form of a red cabbage, n arked "not for competition," exhibited by Mr. J. llrpherd. Generally there is nothing striking about a !Id cabt•age, but one three feet in diameter is soreethinr,' out of the ordinary. It has been humorously suggested that cabbages would do for buttonholes, but surely the humorist would not carry his suggestion to its practical conclusion. In the vegetable, flower and fruit section, potatoes, sweet-peas and peaches respec- tively may be taken as the best. Mention deserves to be made of the collection of vegetables showing a variety of nine, shown by Mr. P. W. Baker. His kidney beans celery, leeks and tomatoes were of very floe

quality. The rivalry for the silver rose bowl given by Messrs. Eustauce and Co., Ltd., was amain very Itt en,but Mr. A. J. Mottram was placed first', Mr. J. Blins'on secured seconi place an Mr. R. Daintith third. Sweet peas were in full force and Lady Greenall's silver flow er howl was again won by Mr. W. Yarwoed who showid nine vases. Cactus dahlias were well spoken of by the judges and svcial mention was made of Mr. J. Owen's exhibits. A special festure was that of the groups of f. liege and flowering plants. Mr. P. Wilkin- son succeeded in securing the first place, Ms groop being far ahead of the other two. The others were characterised by the judges as heing too heavy. The table decorations were really splendid, the first prize heing awarded to Miss E. Hall. The rociety's silver medals for the members obtain- ing most points in the cut flower and vegetable classes were awarded to John T4ylor and Edwin Taylor respectively, while for the _gentlemen's gardeners' medal A. y. Nicholls and .F. J. South were equal.

The following sent exhibits Int not for cot4etition : Mr. I.eonard Davies, carnations ; Miss Olive Acton ild flowers; Mr. S. P. Bolton, pansies; Mr. Peter Cliffe, foliage and other plants ; Mr. C. Plinston,cut blooms; Mr. G. Tandy, group of plants and blooms; Mrs. Massey, group of plants and fruit; and Mr. James flepherd, a large red cabbage. _

the op- ening-ceremony c;:mmenced at 3 o'clock and the bandstand was used as a platform. Sir Gilbert Greenall Bart., presided, and amongst these supporting him were :—Lady Greenall (who opened the fete) Revs. James Collins and H. V. Pigot, Messrs. R. J. Wynne- Jones, Alan Sykes and Vere B. Davies. The Chairmnn said it not only-gave him great pleasure to take the chair, but it bad given him pleasure to be in the proud position of president of the Stockton Heath Garden Society. Their society, he thought he might say without fear of contradiction, was perbaOs the most euterprising.and no doubt the largest in this part of the world. They had a committee N%ho attended the meet- ings with the greatest regularity and they had greatly improved the position of the Scciety. The Society was one that was growing, the members were gradually increasing,and he thought he might say that they should continue to lead against any competitors in this part of the world. The Society's work was not confined only to a one day show as it bad all sorts of Shows—bulb shows etc.—during the year, so that throughout the year there was always some point of interest before tiros() who took an interest in those matters. Sir Gilbert then asked his wife to declare the Show open. Lady Greenall on rising caueed some amusement by addressing her hustand as "Mr. President." Continu- ing she said it was a great pleasure that she was able this year to accept the invita:ion to come there that day, and she was only sorry that in past years she bad not been able to do so. She hoped that they did not expect her to bring a tine day—(laughter)—but they pro- vided a fine day for theWarringt orr Show on Thursday. She wanted to congratulate them on the very good attend- ance, and she was also very pleased 'to see all the children round them looking so pretty. She hoped to be able to see them per form later. • She congratulated them most heartily on the general aspect at the present time of Stockton Heath and its gardens. There was not a manufacturing town In the world that could boast of such a suburb as Stockten Heath was at the present time. The architecture of the }reuses and also the building was very charming, hut however well-built\ a house was it could not look well avithout the he'p of a garden. (Hear, hear.) Concluding she said she wished .to know whether her husband had rioted as president properly. (Laughter.) She had the greatest pleasure in declaring the show open. (Applause.) Miss Mclntyre, a pretty little girl dressed as a gipsy then presented Lady Greenall with a bouquet. The Rev. H. V. Pigot in proposing a vote of thanks to Lady Greenall recalled the fact that he was first president of the Society. Since then they had grown greatly in size and in importance. Proceeding he said he would not flatter Lady Greenall, at she WA S one of the quickest persons he knew for seeing threngh flattery and bunkum.—(laughter)—but she had taken a great interest not only that day, but year in and year out in the Stockton Heath Garden Society. (Applause.) Mr. W. IL J. Jenkins in seconding, said that Mr. Pigot and he felt delighted when they remembered that in his (the speaker's) little Sittingroom they first formed that Society. He was very pleased to see her there that afternoon and he hoped she would be able to give them her presence oftener. (Applause.) Lady Greenall, replying, said she would do everything that lay in her power to forward the Society. Mr. Charles Plinston said he felt exceedingly pleased to propose a vote of thanks to the Chairman, not only for his attendance there that day, but for the very able and courteous manner in v%hich he had conducted their proceedings during the past twelve mouths. When their late presldent, Mr. V. B. Davies, suggested he would like a change they were non-plussed ; they did not know exactly what to do. They knew that Sir Gilbert was a man who was busily occupied up and down the country in respect to agricultural matters, but they had no diffi- culty in getting him as president. Since then every- thing had gone on splendidly. (Applause). Mr. A. Sykes, in seconding, said that when they had Sir Gilbert at the head of affeirs it srelt success, and success bad been spelt there that day. They would say of him that his motto was "Thorough." Sir Gilbert Greenall, resroading, said that it was a great pleasure and privilege in being able to aome there. He had enjoyed the position he had held during the last two months yr ry much, and he had met with universal kindness from everybody.' div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
STRANGE CASE AT WIDNFS. MOTHER AND SON ATTEMPT SUICIDE.

At Widnes Police Court, on Saturday, John Boyd, a Militiaman, and his mother, Fanny 1303 d, of 64, Walnisley-street, were charged with attempting to commit suicide by jumping into the Sanl,ey and S. Helens Canal on Friday. From the evidence it was gathered that the male Prisoner bad just returred from the army and had taken a quantity of drink. This had exasperated the mother, and she spoke to him strongly about it. The male prisoner then jumped out of the house followed by his troller. He climbed over the gate at the Chi rte h use joroth n crossing, and was only saved from a pF,ssing train by his mother taking hold of his coat. He got loose alter tie train had passed, and runn.ng away for a short distarce, he took a running jump into the canal. As he was a good swimmer,tw o m( n tt h o were witnesses of the occurrence had little difficulty in getting him out, His mother remanstrated with him and then. without any warning to the two b3standers, she jur ped in also. With much difficnity she was got out. %Then t9ken into custody shortly afte", John said : "I was in the rats." The bench sympathised with the mother, and dismissed her upon the condition that her s teck care of her The male prisoner wrs remanded for a week to allow the bad effects of the drink to work off.

div.head: Hatton.
div.p: Hatton.

HATTON HORTICULTURAL SOCIETY.—A meeting was held in the Parish Room, Hatton, on Tuesday evening, to distribute prizes to the sac2essful competitors, who turned up in great force. Prize money to the amount of £62 5. ed. was distributed, which is a large amount for a village show. As our re3ders know, the Society was favoured this year with a fine day for once and a record gate was the result. The produce taken cm the whole was very good, some few classes falling below the standard, notably currants and French beans. The poultry classes were a g:tat success, some very fino birds being exhibited. 'The Society are very fortunate in possessing a first class secretary in Mr. G. Hatton, who is never so happy as when be is promoting the wel- fare of the Society. Backed by a zealous committee, the Society will continue to grow and be a credit to the little village of Hatton.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
DRINK AND MEM%

On Saturday at St. Ileleas Police Court, a single woman named Elizabeth Aspnwall, of Hamer-street, was brought up on a charge of stealing a jacket from the shop of Messrs. Drcmgoole and Co., Westfield-street. There were two other charges of stealing a pair of boots from the same shop,and stealing a shoulder of pork from the shop of James Bose, Duke-strect. To all oi which she pleaded guilty. The Chief Constable said that during the past four rcontbs she had been drinking heavily. he was fined 90s. or one months' imprison- ment in each of the three cases.
ST. HELENS CHILD'S DEATH. DOCTOR AND HIS LEGAL RIGHTS.

At St. Helens (::n Monday, Mr. S. Thighouse, county comner, held the inquest on the body of Joseph Norman the newly-born child of John Norman, a collier, of Flag-street, who died on Thursday evening.—Mrs. Whittle said as the chiid appeared iil ale took it to Dr. Bassett. He said he could not attend the baby unless be was paid, and she said she would have to take it back. As she was going to the door be asked what the- nurse wanted him to do. She told him she wanted him to look at it, and be said " Very wpll, I had better look at it,"and he lock- dat it. He then said she would have to tell Norman to take half-a-crown to the surgery at night, and he would attend to it.—'f be Coroner: He. was within his strict legal rights, but whether he was within his On moral rights I will leave to his con- science.—Dr. Unsworth said the car‘e of death was premature birth ; and if it Lad received medical atten- tion it would not have had a chance of recovery.—The jury returned a verdict of" Death from natural causes" and the coroner gave Sergeant Staveley £1 out of his poor-box to expend upon Mrs. Normar, remarking that he must let Norman work for his oun food.

A MINER'S DEATH IN A SEWER. At the St. IlelEns Town Hall, on Monday, Mr. S. Brighouse, county coroner, resumed the inquest on tte hody of Joseph Bray, sixty-three, a miner, of Frederick- street, St. Helens, who was killed by teing buried Ly a fall of clay in the new Sutton sewer which is now 1 eirg constructed for the St. llelens Coiporation. Mr. E. W. Swift represented the contractor, Mr. J. H. Macdonald, of Westminster, and Mr. P. Riley appealed for the relatives.

James Appleton, Harrison-street, Sutton, who ss working with Bray, stated that on the day previous to the accident a motor lurry elunging to Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Cq., came up Edgeworth- street and along Fisher-street. When it turned into Fisher-street it would be about twelve yards from where they were working. It shook the ground so much that they both left their work and came to the bottom of the shaft, lie went up the shaft to see NI bat it was and Bray remarked that the traffic ought to be stopped. Neither of them said any- thing to the foreman atout it. About a quarter eleven on Saturday forenoon he was working at the bottom of the shaft when he heard Bray shout. He went to him, and found that be was on his knees, a bag and a quantity of dirt being on his legs. He managed to raise him to his feet. Another fall came burying him completely. He struggled to the bottom of the shaft, and called for assistance. He was buried by mray tons of clay. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death," and recommended that heavy., traffic should be diverted from the neighbourhood of the senor to such a distance as to prevent any disturbance of the sewer works. The Coroner ssid he would send a copy of that recommendation to the Town Clerk. Mr. Swift said that Mr. Macdonald regretted the accident from every point of view.

div.head: FOISONED CONFECTIONERY.
div.p: FOISONED CONFECTIONERY.

The occurrence of several Cases of poisoning traced to the eating of sweets hes caused widespread alarm vi Rotterdam. Two children have died and tNY') othe.a are so seriously ill that there is little chence of the'r recovery. The police, who are making a close inqu;iy into the affair, have already seized 1,400 Loxes of su-- pccted confectionery.

Warrington Lodging-Houses. Sir,—l am glad to see that someone in Warrington is at least interestedin this subject. I have followed with great interest the clear remarks of" Labor Onmin Tincit ' and there is very much in his letter worthy of every consideration. While I quite agree with him An the main, I am also inclined to think that he is rather overdoing the subject in suggesting that thel Corporation should erect a Central Lodging-House and do away with the old places. This idea would be splendid if it could be carried out, but my Akar " Labor Omnia Vincit " would it be wise to saddle the ratepayers with the cost of snail a building, which might mean an initial outlay of about £2,000? I answer No ! Already the ratepayers of Warrington have quite enough to do to raise the money for the present rates as they are, without perhaps an additional penny or twopence in the pound being added on to it: From what I have heard I believe that the super- vision of these houses at present rests with the Health Department. Would it not be far better if this were left, in the hands of the police? In • other towns I have been in I found that the Lodging House Inspectors were' as a rule police, officers, generally, a sergeant or inspector of police who -visit the houses systemically both day and night ; they are then better able to control them. Such a plan as this would be more advisable in the case of houses where loose characters are known to stop. I believe that these -women are the direct cause of more than one half the troubles, and I for one do not think that the worthy Chief Constable of Warrington would object to the additional work.
Again thanking" you, for your courtesy in this matter.—Yours very faithfully,
FIAT LUX

LAND TAXES WELCOMED.

People Ready to pay more for Luxuries. The Lord Advocate, who has already addressed more meetings in the country in support of the Budget than any other member of the Ministry, and who has sixteen more engagements booked for the next three or four -weeks including Warringten on September 13th, gave a " Daily News "correspondent some interesting impres- sions of the gatherings he has spoken to and the methods he adol.ts to bring the real effect of the Government prcposals before his audiences.• "Two things I have noticed particularry about all my meetings," said Mi. Use "in the first place, they have been of tie most orderly character, and in the second the audiences seemed, so far is r could judge, to be specially interested in the land proposals. They were eager for information on these points and never seemed to weary of detail. "Now I find that the only objection which demands lull and careful consideration Is that the Budget is Socialistic in its tendency. For myself I should-think it is exactly the contrary, but this, of course, depends upon what one understands by Socialism. Aecordingly I always begin by giving my definition of Socialism, which, I may remark, is expressed in the exact words used by Mr. Balfour at Birmingham in 1907. He said Socialism meant the extinction of all private property and the handing of it over to the State. Whenever that definition is carefully grasped it becomes apparent that the land proposals of the Government, so far from confiscating private property, anxiously provide that it shall be respected to the fullest extent, and that a con- tribution for the needs of the State shall be levied only on wealth created by the community. The proposal to tax the value of the land alone and to leave untouched buildings, improvements. and fixed machinery, shows clearly the desire of the Government to secure to every individual the full fruits of his own industry. "Our opponents seem to ire to have forgotten that their own most active supporters liftve put forward taxation of land values as part of their programme, on the express ground that it would form a counter- policy to Socialism, which I think it does. At all events it is clear, and I think as the result of the meetings.cn behalf of the Budget it is row thoroughly grasped by the people, that a proposal to tax lend does not mean that ruthless hands are to be laid upon men's property. In short, it is very difficult to see how taxa- tion on the basis of lard alone is confiscation, if taxa- tion upon land and buildirgs con. bined is accepted as just and fair. VALUATION QUITE EASY. - -

"The Tories seem also to have forgotten that under our present system land is habitually valued apart from the buildings and improvements upon it, especially in the case of factories, workshops and business premises, and the difficulties of valuaticu under the present system are considerably greater than any which are encountered when the problem is the valuation of land alone. It is impossible to convince people that you cannot make a satisfactory valuation of land alone for taxing or rating purposes when it is admitted that a column of irasonry, or a pipe sunk deep in the ground, era pair of rails or telephone posts with wires can be and are habitually valued for rating or taxing purposes under the present system. The hunt after a hypothetical tenant for things such as these is mach more baffling than the hunt for the hypothetical buyer of land alone. "Then again, the ease with which a landed proprietor names his price for such unlikely subjects of commerce aaharren sea-girt rocks or a mud flat covered by water at high tide, when he is asked to sell, throws consider- able doubt upon the proposition that to value such things is irrppssible. "Then again. I have found that the people are not impressed with the argument, which I take care to place clearly before them, that the initial cost of valuation will be great in proportion to the yield of the tax, for they see quite well that this is inevitable, and that as years advance the yield will become greater and the expense considerably less. They seem to understand, however, that the expense of setting up and administer- ing a scientific tariff would be much greater in propor- tion to its yield, and that in the case of the scientific tariff, while the expense would probably increase the yield of the tax would tend to diminish. "In this connection I have been at pains to point out that while an alternative to the Budget is conceivable, none has been, or will be, placed before the country. And I take occasion to remind my audience that the Chamberlain programme is not, and never was intended to be, a revenue-producing plan. Its object was two- fold. First, to consolidate the Empire, and second, to exclude foreign manufacturers from our markets ; and its net result was a heavy deficit which no one had ever suggested or could suggest a means of filling up. Cer- tainly want ofZa business-like alternative to the Budget has proved a fatal kandicap to our political opponents.

div.head: TOBACCO AND WHISKY TAX.
div.p: TOBACCO AND WHISKY TAX.

"What has struck me most of all at my meetings is that perfect equanimity with which the people view the extra duty upon whisky and upon tobacco, especi- ally the latter. They are obviously well pleased to be told that if the Chancellor of the Exchequer's anticipa- tion about the yield of the whisky tax is disappointing it will be all the better for the country, and they make no complaint whatever, so far as I have been able to ascertain, of the extra price which they have to pay for their tobacco. "Lord Lansdowne, in his speech at tteConstitutional Club, stated that unless the Lords were satisfied that the people had had an opportunity of considering and expressing their views about the Budget it would not only be the right but the duty of the Peers to cast it oat. In my view Lord Lansdowne has now had his answer given in the most conclusive way. "While the Government and their supporters have unquestionably spread the light with regard to the Buti3et proposals in all parts of the country, and have received unanimous approval on every occasion when opportunity offered. Lord Lansdowne and his supporters have never explained their hostility to the proposals at any open public meeting and invited an expression of approval of their attitude, except at Manchester, when the result was a little surprising to them. "The result is that the claim now made by the Peers to decide whether or not the people have bad an opportunity to consider the measure, and to express their opinion upon it, is plainly inadmissible ; for they have not taken the means, which the Government and their supporters have done, to find out exactly how public opinion stands. "The answer we have to the Peers is this: 'We have laid our Budget proposals fully before the people and have secured their approval. You have followed no such course. How then can you claim the right to reject the Budject on the ground that the people have not had an opportunity of considering it and express- ing their views upon it ? ' " TO REPLY TO MR. COX.

Mr. Ure concluded by observing that the Budget League campaign would go on for some weeks longer, and he believed the results would be as favourable in the future as they' had been in the past. He was going to address eleven more meetings in England and vas to be at Preston on September 23. He considered the arrangements for the meeting in that large town satis- factory, because the people there would, with the full assent of Mr. Harold Cox, have an opport,pnity of bearing the land clauses of the Finance Bill fully explained and defended, and they would also have an opportunity, which he considered most legitimate, of hearing Mr. Cox make a full reply. "I need scarcely say," concluded the Lord Advocate, "that in my speech at Preston I shall deal at some length with the views which have been at various times expressed by Mr. Cox on the land proposals of the Bullet, both in the House of Commons and in his writings, for in my judgment he is much the ablest critic of that part of the Finance Bill."

div.head: NEW LICENCE DUTIES.
div.p: THE NEW LICENCE DUTIES.
CHANCELLOR'S BUDGET CONCESSIONS.
Important Alteration for Clubs.
The Government's amendments to the licensing clauses Of the Finance Bill were placed on the paper yesterday.

The Chancellor of the Exchequer proposes that the reduced duty in the case of hotels and restaurants where the sales of liquor are less than one-thirdiv4 the hotel receipis should be lowered from 33 per cent. of the compensation value of the premises to 25 per cent., and the original figure of one-tenth of the full duty, below which the amount payable lutist not fall, will be changed to one-thirtieth of the annual value of the premises. It is proposed that the original duty of 3d in the pound on the sales of intoxicating liquor in cluliS shall be changed to a duty of 6d. in the pound on purchases. Mr. Lloyd-George suggests a change in the schedule for spirit and off retailers' licences. The original scale imposed duties from £l4 on licensed premises under an annual value of £3O to £5O on premises of an annual value of over £lOO. The new scale is : Annual value of licensed premises not exceeding 110—£10. Exceeding £lO and not. exceeding £2o—£ll. Exceeding £2O and not exceeding £3o—£ll. Exceeding £2O and not exceeding £5O—Rl5. A separate scale is submitted for wine retailers off-licences, which were originally classed along with the beer retailers'• licences. The new scale for wine retailers' off-licences is :

Annual value of licensed premises hot exceeding £2O —2los. Exceeding £2O, but not exceeding £3o—£3. Exceeding £3O, but not exceeding £so—£3 10s. Exceeding £5O, but not exceeding £7s—£4. div.head: OVER 800 PER CENT. PROFIT.
div.p: OVER 800 PER CENT. PROFIT.
Increment in Which Budget Would
Share.
HOW THE PUBLIC PAY.

One of the most notable cases of the miraculous increase in the value of land let brought to our notice was revealed as the result of a transaction in Denbigh- shire a few years ago, The Birkenhead Town Council wanted 2,000 acres of moorland to extend its new waterworks in Denbighshire by enlarging the reservoirs, &c. The adjoining land, which was well adapted for this purpose, belonged to a Mr. Evans, uho had bought it-3,000 acres in all—for 25,000 a few years previously. The corporation served the usual notice to treat. Mr Evans was prepared to treat—on the basis of receiving £lOO,OOO for two-thirds of the property which had cost him t £5,000. The matter went to arbitration. Sir Edward Clarke was umpire, and, with certain small sums for compensation to displaced tenants, 'he awarded Mr. Evans £27,000 for his 2,000 acres. No doubt the land was worth it, but what a marvellous increase in value, caused in great measure by the com- ing of the water works and the "adaptability" of the land for their extension. Had the Budget land clauses been in operation, the public would have obtained one- fifth of the increment, and the landlord would still have come out of transaction very handsomely. Is this robbery or justice?

div.head: MORE PROGRESSIVE LEGISLATION. State Aid for Farms and Forests.
div.p: MORE PROGRESSIVE LEGISLATION. State Aid for Farms and Forests.
SPECIAL MOTOR ROADS.

In accordance with his promise, Mr. Lloyd-George on Thursday introduced his Development Grant Bill, which embodies certain proposals outlined in his Budget scheme. The Bill, which embodies far-reaching proposals, provides for the making of grants or loans to further forestry agriculture, reclamation of land, the improve- ment and construction of roads, harbours and canals, and the improvement of fisheries. The annual expenditure under he scheme will be about £600,000. . Power is given under the Bill to the Board of Agriculture and Fisheries to acquire compulsorily all land which theyarequire for any purpose, for which a grant is to be made to them. Under the machinery of the Bill, Road Boards will be set up which shall have power to construct new roads for motor traffic on which speed limit laws will not apply: To meet the expense of the construction of these roads the petrol ta; will be allotted to a special fund, which will be supplemented if necessary, by grants. It is believed that a salary of £3,000 per annum will be attached to the office of chairman of the new Road Board which it is proposed to set up.

div.head: TERRIBLE HOIST FATALITY.
div.p: TERRIBLE HOIST FATALITY.
YOUNG MAN KILLED AT THE STORES

Warrington was greatly shocked on Monday morning by the news that a fatal hoist accident had occurred at the new premises of the Co-operative Society in Cairo- street. The victim was William James Taylor, aged 26, of 15, Enville-street, Warrington, who was tiapped while unloading the lift and jammed between the carriage and the blickwork. Death was practically instantaneous. A particularly &id feature of The accident is that Taylor only returned from his holi days the same week-end, and had resumed work on the fatal morning.
(Front a Photograph which was taken cnly last week).
THE LATE MR. TAYLOR

div.head: INQUEST.
div.p: THE INQUEST.

Mr. Coroner Brighouse con-ducted en inquiry into the circumstances attending the death at the Police Station cn Wednesday. Mr. T. S. Steel appeared for the Co-operative Society and Mr. Warren (His Maje,sties Factory Inspec- tor) also watched the proceedings. Mr. Jarman (the secretary of the Scciety) and Mr. J. W. Bibby (com- mittee) were also present. At the commencement of the inquest the Coroner said he had seen the fatal lift work and had &so l'een up end down it himself. He believed that the jury had thoroughly examined it also. . William Taylor, father of the deceased, and a railway guard on the London and North-Western railway proved identification. Qn being asked by the coroner if be had any complaints to lay before the Court as to the accident, witness said be had heard that there was little defect in the working of the lift. He had been given to understand that there was three buttons which worked the lift and one of them was out of order so that it would not work. Be had been told that it was not in working order. The coroner pointed out that the gate would not work unless the two folding doors at the entrance of the lift were closed. When the gates were open the lift could still be worked. Anyone acquainted with the lift would not close the doors but just insert his fingr to the button. On taking the finger away from the button the electric current was disconnected, but if the button happened to stick, after the finger had been removed, the current would still be on and the lift would ascend.
Continuing, the Coroner said the Society would meet all liability that might be incurred. Pir. Steel : Yes and more.

Thomas Hardman, a shop assistant, also employed at the Co-operative Stores, residing at 114, Winwick-road, said that at 10.30 on Monday morning he was engaged with the deceased unloading the lift on the basement of the premises. The lift had previously been loaded from a lurry in the sard. In order to move- the lift a button was pressed which caused it to ascend. When required to stop another button bad to be touched. Sometimes the buttons stuck, but he did not know if they bad done so on this occasion. He did not know if dampness would effect the working of the button.

In answer to Mr. Steel: liVitne-ss had been in the employ of the Society for eight years. Sometimes when the lift was nearly empty they raised it slightly, so as to make it easier to get the boxes Sze. off it. It was perfectly safe to raise the lift if the button were pressed from the inside. The Coroner said that a feasible theory as to how the accident occurred was that the deceased thought it would be easier to raise the lift a little in order to get the goods off. Instead of getting inside the lift and closing the doors he leaned over and pressed the neces- sary button and was trapped whilst leaning over. George Kindon, carter in the employ of the Society, said on hearing a noise made ,by the motor he looked round and saw deceased had been trapped. Witness lowered the lift and extricated deceased.

Mr. R. L. Gass, chief electrical engineer at the Co-operative Wholesale Society, Balloon-street, Man- chester, said he had had a great deal of experience in the construction of lifts. 'There were special provisions for safety in that lift which others of the same type did not contain. It was the most up-to-date lift and the best that could be made. This lift would carry lOcwt. and go at a rate of 70ft.a minute and was worked by tht ee buttons. It was boarded on two sides and the top was covered by a galvanised covering to prevent anything falling from above. The Coroner: Is there anything that could have been done to prevent the accident. Witness: Nothing whatever. The lift was absolutely perfect, and if required to be raised it should have been done from the inside; to do so from the outside was to deliberately disobey instructions. Continuing, he said he thought the accident had occurred through the plunger or button sticking. In reply to Mr. Steel he said he could not give any reason for the plunger sticking. He was, however con- vinced that the deceased knew that it was not quite in working order and took advantage of it. The Coroner: That is a serious allegation to make. Witness : To save himself the trouble of stooping down he raised the lift from the outside. The Coroner :Have you any suggestions to make as to the preservation of life in the future. Witness: Only that those who work the lift should report whenever the lift is out of order. The Coroner wanted to know if there were printed instructions pasted up by the lift. Mr. Jarman in answer said that there were some instructions put up but they were torn down and destroyed.

At this point a juror asked if the plunger could not be placed higher in the woodwork Po that it could only be reached by first entering the lift and thus getting out of the danger zone. Mr. Gass in reply admitted that the lift should not be worked from the outside.

Detective Woollacot (coronei's officer) said he arrived on the scene soon after the accident. He examined the plunger, and took it off and found it corroded. It was stuck, and appeared to have been so for some time. The box which covered the plunger was so rusted that a screw driver had to be used to get it off. The plunger seemed to he permanently jammed and not temporarily. In answer to Mr. Steel, witness said he had seen the lift work since the accident and the plunger again jammed. He thought dampness bad caused it to rust. The witness Hardman was re-called, and in answer to a question from the Coroner he said the plunger had been stuck to his knowledge for about a month. He thought Mr. Rowbottom, the manager of the shop, knew about it.

The inquest was then adjourned for a quarter of an hour in order that Mr. Rowbottom should attend the inquiry. On resuming Mr. Rowbottom said be thought the plunger had been out of order for about three months. He had been told by a man who had previously repaired the lift that the defect was immaterial to the working and safety of the lift. Mr. Gass in reply, said that the workman wouldn't say such a thing. Mr. Rowbottom then intimated that he was under the impression that he made such a statment. In answer to Mr. Steel, witness said the employees had no need to rush over their work as they were not on piece work. The reason why he did not report the matter to Mr. Atkinson was that he did not think it was of sufficient importance. The Coroner said that in his opinion if the plunger had been in working order the accident would not have happened. He attached no blame to the Society who be knew would do all they could to ensure the safety of their workmen. He was extremely sorry for Mr. Taylor shom he knew, very well with being a guard on the railway and be was sorry he had lost his lad. He suggested that the inspection of the lift should be put into the hands of one of the employees whose duty it would be to report upon it whenever it went out of order. The jury retired and on their return the foreman said that death was accidental. They attached no blame to anyone and also added that a truck should be pro- vided so as to take heavy boxes from the lift and that a non-corrosive metal box pe used to cover the plunger and that a periodical inspection be made of the lift and its workings. Mr. Steel on behalf of the Society, said, that two of the recommendations made by the jury were already in force, that of having trucks ready for removing heavy boxes. With regard to the non-corrosive box it had been fixed up. The other suggestion would receive consideration. He had to express to the parents and relatives deep sympathy on the fatal accident, which was the first one that the Society had had in 41 years. The committee felt most deeply for the parents. As far as money could help, disregarding the legal respon- sibility, they would be most liberal. He also intimated that the committee were holding a private meeting that night when the matter would be gone into.

div.head: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
div.p: ROYAL COURT THEATRE.
" Rollicking Rory."

" Rollicking Rory " is a rollicking story of typical Irish life. It is not a modern nor a serious story— far from it - but in many passages one's blood is stirred by the outrageous conduct of Stephen D'Arcy, described as a moneylender, in the person of Mr. Carthage Caldclemzh. The play opens with a love scene between Widow O'Donohoe (Miss Jeanette Lyons) and Sergeant Callaghan (Mr. Edward Lowrie). The latter avows his passion openly and enthusiasti- cally,but the widow is coy. In the midst of their amour Rosie Callagan (Miss Nana Flensburg) appears on the scene and the others leave. She is waiting for Rory- O'Donohoe (Mr. Chalmers Mackey) known as Rollick- ing Rory. She hears his footstep and thinking to spring a surprise upon him she hides. Rory comes along and swears he has seen her. "It must have been her ghost," he cries, "but I dont believe in ghosts. However, lam a firm believer in spirits' —a sentiment which he proved to be true by emptying a glass of the same. Another scene is presented in which D'Arcy asks Captain Ashleigh (Mr. Fred Charles) if he would like the loan of some money. Ashleigh' replies that he is now inde- pendent and that in his wardrobe at the present time are 500 guineas. D'Arcy along with his "slave," 'Shaun Brady (Mr. St. John Stuart) 'get the money and also take away little Rosaleen, Captain Ashleigh's five-year-old daughter. At the loss of her only child Mrs. Ashleigh dies and Rosaleen is brought up by D'Arcy and goes under the name of Grace. Fifteen years later she falls in love with Desmond Fitzgerald, an Irish gentleman pro- scribed and outlawed. D'Arcy is guardian to Desmond and successor to the estate, and desiring money, he has a warrant issued for his arrest on the plea that he is false to his country. Desmond makes his escape at the warning of Grace and in due time they are married and she is restored to her father. During all these happenings Rory is a foremost personage, his many jokes, seeming to be made in all seriousness, delight those who pay a visit to the theatre. All the actors play their parts well. Mr. Chalmers Mackey makes an inimitable and irrepressible Rory. The villain of the piece is admirably pourtrayed by Mr. Caldcleugh as D'Arcy. The parts of Captain Ashleigh's wife, and Grace D'Arcy, are played with spirit and taste by Mrs. Chalmers Mackey. Miss Nana Flensburg's bright style is well suited to the role of Rosie Callaghan who subsequently marries the hero, Rollicking Rory. -
NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME. MISS LANCASHIRE LTD.

The above famous farce has previously won an enviable reputation among Warrington playgoers, and they can ,be relied upon to give a hearty welcome next week to Miss Florence Baines on her first appearance in England after a world-tour. "Miss Lancashire Ltd." has come back replete with new songs and new dances, and Miss Baines is announced to sing her enormously successful song "Snowball." The orchestra will be specially augmented for the occasion, and be under the direction of Mr. William Benson.

div.head: SHOOTING MATCH.
div.p: SHOOTING MATCH.
APPLETON RIFLE CLUB v. DARESBURY RIFLE CLUB.

A team of nine members of the Appleton Rifle Club visited Daresbury on Saturday last for the purpose of competing in a rifle shooting match with the Daresbury Rifle Club, whose range is situated in a gunny similar in many respects to the one at Appleton, The light was not very good for shooting but a most keenly con- tested match took place during which some very credi- table scores were made on both sides. The conditions were as follows :—Each team to consist of nine members the best eight scores on each side to count, miniature rifles, ten shots at each of three ranges, 25, 50, and 100 yards. Decimal scoring. Highest possible at each range 100 per man, or an aggregate of 300 for the three ranges. The match resulted in a victory for the Appleton Club, who made a total of 1,927 against 1,805 by the Daresbury Club, the former thus winning by a majority of 122. The following scores were made.

div.head: NEW FLYING RECORDS.
div.p: NEW FLYING RECORDS.
Mr. Latham Flies 95 Miles at
Express Speed.
Another aerial record was established at Rheims on Thursday.

This time the honour was secured by Mr. Latham, who broke all records for speed and distance by flying 95 miles in 2 hours 18 minutes, the previous best being M. Paulhan's 82 miles in 2 hours 43 minutes, accomplished on Wednesday. The flight was watched by thousands of spectators, and Mr. Latlytm was enthusiastically cheered. In the course of his journey the aviator easily beat a Paris express, and at one time had to manceuvre in a storm.

div.head: Education Committee.
div.p: Education Committee.

A meeting of the Education Committee will be held in the Council Chamber, Town Hall, on Monday evening at six o'clock. The minutes of the School Management Committee contain a resolution that Miss Hannah Rowland be appointed a certificated assistant mistress in the Girls' Department of tht? Bolton Council echoul, at a commencing salary at the rate of £BO per annum; her engagement to commence on the Ist October, 1909.—0 n the recommendation of the Managers of the Bolton School, it was also resolved that the Rev. G. C. Briggs, M.A., and Mr. F. R. Roberts be appointed Manigers of that school.—A return shewing the attendance of scholars from the public elementary schools at .the Special Subjects' Centres during the year 1908-9 was submitted, and it was noted (a) Handicraft Centre—that 202 boys had attended from six schools, 195 of whom had attended with'sufficient regularity to qualify for grant; and (b) Cookery, Centres—that 470 girls had received instruction in the second and 680 in the first course of instruction-1,150 in all.—Councillor Steel will move "that resolution 02494 referring to the termination of Mrs. Langdon Isabel Cann's engagement as Superin- tendent of Cookery Instruction on the 31st August next, be rescinded."
An inmate of the,Winchester Workhouse has written to the master to the effect that unless he is supplied with tobacco, sugar and tea he will not remain in the "house."

A jewellery robbery has been committed in one of the larger hotels in Harrogate. During the temporary absence of a lady visitor her bedroom was entered and close upon £lOO worth of jewellery was taken.

THE FUNERAL. Impressive scenes were witnessed at the funeral which took place at the Warrington Cemetery on Thursday afternoon. En route large crowds congregated to a it- ness it and at the Cemetery about 2,000 friends and sympathisers paid their last tribute to the deceased. Almost all of the employees of .the different branches of the Society in Warrington attended and walked in procession in front of the hearse. Mr. J. W. Bibby (member of the committee), Mr. Jarman (secretary), and Mr. T. S. Steel (solicitor) represented the Society, There were large numbers of wreaths sent by relatives and friends, among which were four sent by the Society, one from his fellow workmen and one from the Co-operative Employment Association of which deceaked was a member. At the graveside, the combined mem- bers of the Apollo and Co-operative Choirs (of which deceased belonged) effectively sang Farewell my own true love." The Rev. H. B. Virth, vicar of St. James' conducted the service, which was of a most impressive and touching character.
